# Audit Report

## Executive Summary

The audit reveals 1,567 findings across the codebase, exposing a tension between conceptual design assumptions and observational contract realities. Conceptual design flaws—specifically a zero-cost complexity posture and unbudgeted report synthesis—have created ~17.5k lines of untyped governance machinery while overwhelming deliverables with single-lens maintainability noise. Concurrently, observational contract assessments surfaced critical vulnerabilities in execution sandboxing, quote grounding, state concurrency, and test suite fidelity that undermine the system's core trust guarantees.

## Summary

- Findings: 1567
- Work blocks: 4
- Severity breakdown: critical: 2, high: 31, medium: 865, low: 652, info: 17
- Lens breakdown: architecture: 84, config_deployment: 5, correctness: 113, data_integrity: 45, maintainability: 1102, observability: 1, operability: 2, performance: 9, reliability: 28, security: 13, tests: 165
- Grounding (S7): grounded: 443
- Fully audited files: 25
- Excluded non-auditable files: 191

## Top Risks

- Arbitrary code execution on auditor host via untrusted repository imports, root binary shadowing, attached git short-flag bypasses, and un-sandboxed shell commands.
- False-confidence verification where single-character quote matches or model-authored predicates mark ungrounded or hallucinated claims as adversarially verified.
- Silent execution drift and invalidation cascades caused by unpinned working trees during long-running audit sessions.
- State loss and race conditions in remediation workflows due to non-atomic state overrides (saveState) lacking TOCTOU protection.
- Governance lock and maintainability drag caused by ~17.5k lines of untyped, fragile enforcement scripts blocking core usability and CI reliability.

## Themes

### T-001 — Observational Contract Assessment: Untrusted Producer Execution & Boundary Bypasses

- Root cause: The runtime architecture fails to enforce strict execution boundaries, allowing untrusted producer inputs (audited repo code, repo-root binaries, attached git flags, and LLM-authored strings) to execute with host privileges.
- Findings: ARC-e536e502, ARC-1ec7c91d, COR-14fcd42a, COR-bbdae93c, SEC-2975f558, ARC-eb0f6110-2, SEC-f775b8ae, SEC-aafe02b8
- Suggested fix pattern: Isolate dependency resolution to version-keyed tool caches, enforce bare allowlisted binary tokens with path verification, fence untrusted target-repo text in non-forgeable data envelopes, and mandate pinned releases for external analyzers.

### T-002 — Conceptual Design Critique: Governance Hypertrophy & Unpriced Complexity

- Root cause: A foundational philosophy treating complexity as zero-cost generated ~17.5k lines of untyped governance scripts and invasive user-facing friction gates while core operational pathways remain unbudgeted and unverified.
- Findings: ARC-d6d51109, ARC-eaffc6ab, ARC-94d4181f, ARC-908bbca5, ARC-908bbca5-2, ARC-a07ca298, ARC-9111aa7c, ARC-15fb5ae5
- Suggested fix pattern: Re-establish complexity as a formal design cost in decision gates, consolidate doc-linting into single declarative scripts, bring enforcement scripts under typechecking, and reorder intake gates so repo analysis precedes configuration.

### T-003 — Observational Contract Assessment: Weak Verification & Synthetic Grounding Deficits

- Root cause: Verification mechanisms (grounding, anchor confirmation, write-scope enforcement) validate syntactic existence or model self-reports rather than semantic correctness, allowing empty quotes or model predicates to launder unverified claims.
- Findings: ARC-60a52950, ARC-60a52950-2, ARC-182085b7, ARC-1da979b7-3, ARC-eb0f6110, ARC-e4912d83, ARC-e362503b, ARC-c9869af2
- Suggested fix pattern: Mandate distinctive quote spans matched against cited line ranges, prevent model-chosen predicates from overriding tier-1 grounding failures, stamp verified reviewer identities on artifacts, and enforce strict worktree write-confinement.

### T-004 — Observational Contract Assessment: Unpinned Scope Continuity & Concurrency Risk

- Root cause: The continuity model lacks run-level git SHA pinning to prevent staleness cascades during long runs, while state persistence primitives rely on unsafe full-object overrides without TOCTOU or concurrency locks.
- Findings: ARC-b38f2c8a, ARC-479f5151, ARC-c7128577, ARC-017d52ff, COR-e93ec2d4, ARC-479f5151-2, ARC-6fe6e301
- Suggested fix pattern: Pin target repository revisions at run initialization, enforce bidirectional DAG-to-registry consistency in contract tests, replace saveState with lock-held atomic mutation primitives, and validate performance on external benchmark repositories.

### T-005 — Conceptual Design Critique: Unbounded Report Aggregation & Hidden Degradation

- Root cause: The reporting design lacks per-lens yield caps and finding aggregation, allowing thousands of low-severity maintainability observations to drown critical risks in a 1.29 MB deliverable while parser failures remain undisclosed.
- Findings: ARC-1da979b7, ARC-1da979b7-2, ARC-2975f558, ARC-0e0a0b44, ARC-cc6091dd
- Suggested fix pattern: Adopt standard SARIF ingestion, roll up multi-site pattern instances into aggregated findings, budget the human-facing report to executive summaries and top risks, and explicitly disclose parse-tier degradations in report metadata.

### T-006 — Observational Contract Assessment: Test Suite Decay & Vacuous Verification

- Root cause: Contract test suites rely on local re-implementations, unasserted setup conditions, or retired directory paths, producing false-green suite passes that mask underlying runtime defects.
- Findings: TST-c0c52641, TST-70b39a91, TST-5398b45a, TST-e756b905, TST-09e5b348, TST-0e3fc2e0, TST-0fd4fb71-2, TST-fa0b2971, TST-547182c1, TST-daffae23, TST-00a78517, TST-4259172a, TST-7af75d05, TST-caab6d8f
- Suggested fix pattern: Refactor test suites to exercise actual production code paths rather than local copies, add cross-platform CI matrix testing, fail loudly on setup step errors, and update path invariants to match current project layouts.

### ARC-e536e502 — Execution authority is inherited from untrusted producers: the audited repo and the model's own output both decide what code runs, in-process and via shell

Raised by one perspective (adversary) and admitted on evidence, not consensus: it is the highest-impact finding in the review.

- Severity: critical
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/shared/tooling/analyzerDeps.ts`, `src/audit/extractors/analyzers/typescript.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/localCommands.ts`, `src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts` +5 more
- Details: Raised by one perspective (adversary) and admitted on evidence, not consensus: it is the highest-impact finding in the review. The unstated, false assumption is that the things which SUPPLY the tool — the repository under audit, and the LLM output the tool consumes — are trusted to determine what executes. The tool rigorously validates the SHAPE of producer output (schemas, grounding, reviewed_clean) and never asks whether a producer has the authority to cause execution. Six verified instances, one defect class. (a) In-process import() of repo JavaScript: resolveAnalyzerDep prefers the AUDITED repo's node_modules before the shared cache (src/shared/tooling/analyzerDeps.ts:121-126), that path becomes dependencyPath (graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:126), and typescript.ts:40-51 reads the repo's typescript/package.json, takes manifest.main, and awaits import(pathToFileURL(...)) — unsandboxed, in the auditor's process, with the entry field attacker-controlled and fed to resolve/join so it need not stay inside the package; treeSitter.ts:70-85 does the same. The wrapping try/catch (graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:134-140) turns any throw into a cosmetic analyzer note, so a payload that runs and then throws reads as benign degradation. This is the DEFAULT path — settingFor yields auto when unset (registry.ts:66-71) and the conversation-first rule means the user sets no flags. (b) Repo-root executable shadowing: resolveCandidate falls back to join(root, candidate.command) and spawns it with cwd=root, env=process.env, no timeout (src/audit/orchestrator/localCommands.ts:98-126), so a repo shipping an executable named prettier/black/gofmt/python/npx at its root gets it run when the real tool is off PATH. (c) The default-deny allowlist is bypassable by path prefix: executableBaseName strips directories via split('/').pop() (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:214-223), so argv ['src/grep','-n','x'] base-names to grep, passes, and spawns with cwd = repo root. (d) Ecosystem runners execute repo build code by design (npx -y, pipx run, cargo, bundle exec at acquisitionEngine.ts:172-183,350) with nothing pinning --no-install/--offline/--locked and no timeout or output cap. (e) LLM-authored command strings reach a shell: test_command/e2e_command are accepted behind only a typeof string check (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:1638-1641) then spawnSync(..., {shell:true}) (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:885-890, :996-1001), as are targeted_commands sourced from the audit report (worktreeLifecycle.ts:257-262); the filters are heuristic DENYLISTS with no executable allowlist. These are the only three shell:true sites in src/ and all three carry non-tool-authored strings. (f) Blast radius is amplified because the env scrub removes only CLAUDECODE, /^CLAUDE_CODE/ and AUDIT_TOOLS_CALLER_CWD (src/shared/tooling/exec.ts:306-320), so every provider API key and GITHUB_TOKEN is inherited by every child. What makes this design rather than a bug list is where the boundary WAS drawn: the path reaching the NETWORK is rigorous (fixed vendor URLs, sha256 verification, an admitSpawn chokepoint, only gitleaks admitted by default) while the paths reaching the untrusted input itself have no gate — admitSpawn cannot help with (a) because that is import(), not spawn, and consent_token is an existence check rather than an authorization (any non-blank string admits every non-default candidate, acquisitionEngine.ts:216-225). Fix as a class: resolve analyzer dependencies from the shared version-keyed cache or the tool's own install and NEVER from the audited tree (read a needed version from the manifest and installToCache it); drop the repo-root fallback in resolveCandidate; base-name only after rejecting any token containing a path separator; route the three shell:true sites through argv plus the existing allowlist so a model-supplied command is authorized rather than merely un-denylisted; scrub the child env to a declared passlist. Then write down the threat model — a repo-wide grep for 'threat model' returns nothing, and a tool whose purpose is pointing at code you have reason to distrust needs a stated answer to what the audited repo is allowed to do to us. The answer is already written for downloaded binaries.
- Evidence: 4 items (top: "runtime:flow:flow:host:external-analyzer-acquisition: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### ARC-b38f2c8a — Nothing pins the revision under audit, so the continuity model silently assumes a frozen tree and punishes the long runs it was built for

Raised independently by two perspectives (pragmatist, adversary) with non-overlapping evidence, which is the strongest corroboration in the review.

- Severity: critical
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/fileIntegrity.ts`, `src/shared/providers/reviewSnapshot.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts` +4 more
- Details: Raised independently by two perspectives (pragmatist, adversary) with non-overlapping evidence, which is the strongest corroboration in the review. The load-bearing unexamined assumption of the whole artifact model is that the audited tree does not change during a run; nothing enforces or even records it. There is no run-level revision pin anywhere in the audit half — no pinned_revision/git_sha/head_sha/snapshotSha field in src/shared/types/sessionConfig.ts, src/audit/types/auditScope.ts, or the run ledger — so every extraction reads the live working tree. Drift IS detected: checkFileIntegrity re-hashes a task's files against recorded manifest hashes (src/audit/orchestrator/fileIntegrity.ts:19-62). The handling is the most expensive available: on !integrity.is_clean, nextStepHelpers.ts:2646-2658 re-runs intake, which re-extracts repo_manifest, whose content hash changes, which cascades the staleness DAG through the planning chain (repo_manifest is a declared input to audit_tasks.json, charter_register.json and coverage_matrix.json per spec/audit/dependency-map.md:37-107). The project's own records confirm the observed consequence: docs/HANDOFF.md instructs laps to land work WITHOUT a run because a commit mid-run re-stales the planning chain and regresses it to charter_extraction, and docs/backlog/open-bugs.md:511 records a real 313-packet run invalidated exactly that way. This is the expected case, not an edge: every property the design is proud of pushes runs toward being LONG (bounded per-invocation steps, resumability across sessions, quota pacing that deliberately waits for windows to reset, cooperative peers). Secondary cost: cross-wave incommensurability — wave 1 and wave 2 can review different trees and their findings merge as if describing one codebase — and A9 (peers joining one run) is incoherent without an agreed answer to which tree the run is about. This is also the mechanical reason the project has no clean validation evidence (see DR-003): developing the tool and validating it on itself are mutually exclusive. Stated precisely so it is not overclaimed: the citation half is already largely defended, because quote grounding matches on CONTENT not line numbers (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:158-193), so findings survive line shifts. The machinery for the fix also already exists with the wrong lifetime: createReviewSnapshot does git worktree add --detach HEAD (src/shared/providers/reviewSnapshot.ts:104) but is torn down per drive, and src/remediate/steps/dispatch/worktreeLifecycle.ts is a 900-line worktree substrate that already adds at HEAD and copies gitignored files over. Capture one revision at run start, record it in the run ledger as the run's identity, and resolve every read through it. A moved HEAD then becomes an explicit operator decision (continue against the pinned revision, or re-baseline) instead of an invisible staleness cascade. This is the cheapest-now/expensive-later item in the review: retrofitting later means re-basing the provenance of every artifact hash and every anchor. Non-git targets keep today's behavior.
- Evidence: 6 items (top: "runtime:flow:flow:host:artifact-staleness-dag: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### ARC-d6d51109 — (judge-added) The standing decision that effort and complexity are not costs removed the only brake on the accretion this entire review is measuring

No perspective questioned this, and it is the generative cause behind a large fraction of what all five independently found.

- Severity: high
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `docs/project-philosophy.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/design-check/SKILL.md`, `package.json`
- Details: No perspective questioned this, and it is the generative cause behind a large fraction of what all five independently found. docs/project-philosophy.md:74 and :245 state, as a standing preference, that effort, complexity and refactor size are NOT costs — only the eventual endpoint matters — and CLAUDE.md repeats it with the instruction never to defer or pick a lighter half-measure because the ideal is a lot of work. That rule is correct as an answer to the question it was written for (do not ship a half-measure to save labor). But it was generalized into a claim about complexity itself, and complexity is a cost that is paid by every future reader and every future mechanism, not by the author at the moment of the change. With that cost declared to be zero, nothing in the project's decision procedure ever argues against adding a mechanism. The aggregate result is measurable and is what the other 44 findings describe from five different angles: 23 verify legs of which 11 police the project's own prose (DR-018), ~17,500 lines of enforcement machinery outside any typechecker (DR-019), 26 parity/drift tests standing in for extraction the project's own rule prefers (DR-023), 13 hooks, a guard-reach registry, a doc manifest, an attestation system, four separate drain ceilings, five hand-authored materializations of one obligation relation (DR-010), ~179,300 lines of tests against ~143,700 lines of source, and a 1.29 MB deliverable nobody can read (DR-012) — for a tool with two commands and one user. Note the asymmetry the short-attention perspective isolated independently: the parts a USER touches (step prompts, step contracts, the report's first 90 lines) are consistently well-budgeted, while the parts only a MAINTAINER touches are consistently not. That is exactly what a zero-cost-complexity rule predicts, because a user-facing budget has an external forcing function and an internal one has none. The project already proves it can price complexity when it decides to: check:backlog-budget exists precisely because backlog entries grew past navigability, and MAX_DRAIN_STEPS, DEFAULT_SCOPE_MAX_FILES and the packet budget cap are all deliberate ceilings on the product's own behavior. Recommendation, framed as a decision for the owner rather than a defect: narrow the rule to what it was for — do not trade the correct endpoint for less labor — and restore complexity as a real cost in the design gate, so that 'this adds a mechanism a future reader must hold' counts against a change, and 'this deletes one' counts for it. Concretely, extend the /design-check gate to require that a change proposing a new mechanism name what it deletes, and point the existing budget-gate mechanism at the internal surfaces (CLAUDE.md, the gate roster, the hook roster) that currently have no ceiling. Without this, every recommendation in this review that says 'add a mechanism' makes the problem worse, and every one that says 'delete two and derive the third' will keep losing to the rule as written.

### ARC-60a52950 — (judge-added) What the tool calls verification proves only that a quoted span exists; the tier that could establish falsity never fired, and 61 grounded verdicts carry no quote at all

Every perspective either credited quote-grounding as the North Star correctly implemented (adversary, explicitly) or complained about how it is TALLIED (pragmatist, DR-006).

- Severity: high
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts`, `src/shared/types/finding.ts`, `src/audit/reporting/synthesis.ts`, `.audit-tools/audit-findings.json` +2 more
- Details: Every perspective either credited quote-grounding as the North Star correctly implemented (adversary, explicitly) or complained about how it is TALLIED (pragmatist, DR-006). None asked what the property actually establishes, and the answer changes how much of the product's trust claim survives. Grounding is defined in src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts: a finding is grounded as soon as ONE of its affected_files[].quoted_text spans re-reads from its cited file, content-matched with whitespace/CRLF normalization (:158-193). That proves the cited code EXISTS. It does not evaluate the claim made about the code. The schema carries a second, stronger tier — status refuted means an executable anchor DISPROVED the claim (src/shared/types/finding.ts:57,63) — and that is the only mechanism in the pipeline that can establish a finding is false. On the committed 1480-finding self-audit it fired zero times: 0 refuted, and 0 findings carry any runtime_validation or anchor field at all (verified by direct scan of .audit-tools/audit-findings.json; summary.runtime_validation_status_breakdown is absent). So in practice 'verified' means 'the quote exists', while README.md:85-86 says 'adversarially verified' and the README's own illustrative sample advertises a verdict vocabulary the contract has no field for (186 verified-real of 204 extracted, 10 false, 8 uncertain). Second, the weak property is not even internally consistent in the shipped artifact: 61 of the 436 findings marked grounded carry no non-empty quoted_text on any affected_files entry (386 of 1480 findings carry a quote at all), which the module's own stated rule says must be ungrounded — a finding that carries no quote at all is ungrounded. Either those verdicts are wrong, or the evidence backing them was discarded when the contract was written; both are defects, and nothing checks either. Why this is the deeper half of DR-006: fixing the tally so the counts sum to 1480 makes the report honest about HOW MANY findings were checked, while leaving the reader to believe that a checked finding was assessed for truth. Recommendation: (1) add a contract invariant, enforced at ingest and in the validator rather than by a producer, that status==='grounded' requires either a re-verifiable quote present in the persisted record or an anchor verdict — so the 61 cannot exist; (2) rename the reported bucket to what it measures (citation_verified) and state in the render that it is an existence check, not a truth check; (3) treat the A2 oracle corpus (docs/backlog/forward-tracks.md:108-126, which already reasons correctly that labeling only what the tool FOUND measures precision while recall needs ground truth the tool did not author) as the only instrument that can measure the property the product actually claims, and gate release on it. Until something measures finding precision, the whole verification apparatus is optimizing a proxy — and DR-013's 1138 maintainability findings versus 1 security finding is what an unmeasured proxy looks like from outside.
- Evidence: 3 items (top: "runtime:flow:flow:host:synthesis-report-emission: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### ARC-1ec7c91d — Anchor allowlist pins the executable NAME, not the binary: a repo-local `grep.cmd` is admitted and run through cmd.exe with cwd set to the audited repo

INFERRED CONTRACT: two explicit safety claims.

- Severity: high
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts`, `src/shared/tooling/exec.ts`, `src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts`, `tests/shared/allowlisted-exec.test.ts`
- Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: two explicit safety claims. (1) only "inspection-only executables" may run — `isAllowedAnchorCommand` is "the single authority for what the tool will auto-run on the model's behalf" (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:286-294); (2) commands "run only via `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand`, which spawns argv-only (never a shell)" (allowlistedExec.ts:22-24, repeated at :322-324). The module was hardened once already against CVE-2024-27980, so the threat model is acknowledged.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the allowlist validates a *derived name* while the runner spawns the *caller's original string*. `executableBaseName` strips any directory and then strips a `.cmd`/`.bat`/`.exe` suffix (allowlistedExec.ts:215-223); `isAllowedAnchorCommand` matches that basename (:298-303); but `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand` spawns `resolveExecArgv(command)` built from the untouched `command[0]` (:339-340). Verified by running the shipped code:
  `["./grep.cmd","x","."]`             → allowed: true → spawns `["C:\\Windows\\system32\\cmd.exe","/d","/s","/c","./grep.cmd x ."]`
  `["grep.bat","x"]`                   → allowed: true → spawns via cmd.exe
  `["C:/tmp/evil/git.exe","log"]`      → allowed: true → spawns that exact binary
  `["tools/rg","x"]`                   → allowed: true → spawns `tools/rg`
So BOTH claims fail. The identity claim fails because any path whose last segment matches after suffix-stripping is admitted — the allowlist constrains what the file is *called*, not what it is. The "never a shell" claim fails on win32 because `resolveExecArgv` → `wrapForWindowsBatch` (src/shared/tooling/exec.ts:238-248) routes any `.cmd`/`.bat` through `cmd.exe /d /s /c`, which is a command interpreter. (The `quoteForCmd` hardening is sound and does neutralize metacharacter injection — the gap here is executable identity and the shell hop, not quoting.)

WHY IT MATTERS: `runAllowlistedReadOnlyCommand` is called with `cwd = repoRoot` (anchorGrounding.ts:178), i.e. the repository being audited, and audit-code's purpose is auditing codebases it does not own. cmd.exe resolves a relative command against its own cwd, so `./grep.cmd` denotes a file in the *untrusted* repository. A repo containing a `grep.cmd`/`git.bat` plus an anchor naming it therefore executes repo-supplied code at ingest, with only the `CLAUDE_CODE*` env stripped. The existing `admitSpawn` consent gate shows the project already treats repo-triggered subprocess execution as requiring consent; this path has no such gate. Note the test suite explicitly blesses a path-shaped executable (`["/usr/bin/grep","x"]` at tests/shared/allowlisted-exec.test.ts:64 / tests/audit/anchor-grounding.test.ts:64) and no test covers a `.cmd`/`.bat`/relative-path form, so the gap is uncovered rather than known-accepted.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: require `command[0]` to be a bare token (no `/`, `\`, or drive letter) and to match an allowlisted name with NO suffix stripping; resolve it to an absolute path yourself against a trusted PATH and spawn that resolved path. Refuse a `.cmd`/`.bat` target outright rather than wrapping it, so the "never a shell" invariant holds on win32 too. Add the adversarial cases above as refusal tests beside the existing ones.
- Evidence: 3 items (top: "runtime:unit:src-audit: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### ARC-94d4181f — audit-tools/shared is a single flat barrel of 1,041 re-exports, so the shared core has no internal boundaries — and quota-to-providers is a real runtime import cycle nobody can see

Two perspectives found this independently; the mathematician's evidence is decisive because it names a concrete violation the barrel conceals.

- Severity: high
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/shared/index.ts`, `src/shared/quota/apiPool.ts`, `src/shared/providers/sharedProviderConfirmation.ts`, `src/shared/providers/identity.ts` +3 more
- Details: Two perspectives found this independently; the mathematician's evidence is decisive because it names a concrete violation the barrel conceals. src/shared/index.ts is 1,531 lines re-exporting 1,041 named symbols across 277 export blocks, and it is the only realistic way to consume the shared area: 587 import sites use the barrel, only 10 use the shared/* subpath package.json already publishes, and tests reach past both with 322 deep-relative ../../src/shared/... imports — three coexisting idioms for one dependency, with the same module imported both ways (tests/audit/quota-file-lock.test.ts uses the subpath while tests/remediate/quota-file-lock.test.ts imports the same functions from the barrel). Two concrete consequences. First, the barrel has become a maintained artifact with its own drift test: tests/shared/shared-tests-invariants.test.mjs contains seven assertions (INV-shared-tests-07) whose entire content is that named symbols still appear in the barrel. - Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: `anchorGrounding.ts` states it plainly — "the confirmed bit is the tool's run — never the model's word" (src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:9-10). The tier-2 anchor pass exists precisely because tier-1 cannot verify a *behavior* claim, and the docstring cites real hallucinated findings (a fabricated dependency cycle) that only a deterministic re-run caught.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the finding supplies BOTH halves of the experiment. `finding.executable_anchor.command` is model-authored AND `finding.executable_anchor.confirm_if` — the predicate that decides confirmed-vs-refuted — is also model-authored. Nothing anywhere relates the command to the claim. So the model can pick any command/predicate pair that is true by construction. Verified by running the shipped code: `isAllowedAnchorCommand(["git","log","-1"])` → true, and `confirm_if: {kind: "exit_zero"}` makes `evaluateExpectation` (anchorGrounding.ts:116-120) return `confirmed: true` on any repo with a commit. `["git","rev-parse","HEAD"]` and `["git","status"]` are likewise admitted and likewise always exit 0. The `output_excludes` kind is even cheaper: any text unlikely to appear in the output confirms.

AMPLIFIER: `combineGroundingWithAnchor` (anchorGrounding.ts:226) promotes a confirmed anchor to `{status: "grounded"}` UNCONDITIONALLY, discarding the tier-1 verdict — verified: `combineGroundingWithAnchor({status:"ungrounded",reason:"quote not found on disk"}, {status:"confirmed"})` returns `{"status":"grounded"}`. So a self-confirming anchor LAUNDERS a finding whose cited code does not exist from `ungrounded` into `grounded`. The consequence is not cosmetic: `findingIsGrounded` (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:207) is what the remediator consults, and `groundingVerificationBullet` (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/implementPrompt.ts:328) returns an empty string for a grounded finding — so the "VERIFY BEFORE FIX" instruction is suppressed and a remediation worker applies a fix to a fabricated claim without re-checking. This inverts INV-GND-02, whose whole point is that a missing verdict must never be mistaken for a passing one.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: treat a model-chosen predicate as untrusted. Either (a) restrict `confirm_if` to kinds the tool derives from the claim rather than the model (e.g. the anchor must reference the finding's own cited path/symbol, and `exit_zero` on a command with no relation to the claim is refused), or (b) stop letting an anchor OVERRIDE a failed tier-1: make `grounded` require tier-1 to pass, and let a confirming anchor only ADD evidence. Option (b) is the smaller change and restores the invariant that the tool's own re-read is the floor. At minimum, record the anchor verdict as a separate field rather than collapsing it into `grounding.status`, so a downstream consumer can tell "quote re-verified" from "the model's own predicate passed".

### ARC-60a52950-2 — Quote-and-verify grounding admits any non-empty span, so a one-character quote grounds any fabricated finding

INFERRED CONTRACT: the S7 anti-hallucination gate.

- Severity: high
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts`, `src/audit/validation/quoteGrounding.ts`, `src/audit/reporting/synthesis.ts`
- Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: the S7 anti-hallucination gate. "every finding cites a verbatim span (`affected_files[].quoted_text`); the tool re-reads that span from disk and content-matches it... a quote naming code that does not exist cannot match" (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:5-13). The safeguard is explicitly "attached to the *claim*".

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the only threshold on the cited span is non-blankness — `typeof loc.quoted_text === "string" && loc.quoted_text.trim().length > 0` (findingGrounding.ts:169) — and the match is a substring test over whitespace-collapsed text (`quoteMatches`, findingGrounding.ts:144-148). There is no minimum length, no distinctiveness/entropy requirement, and no check that the span is anywhere near the finding's claimed `line_start`/`line_end`. Grepped the whole tree: no `MIN_QUOTE`/quote-length constant exists anywhere. Verified by running the shipped code against a real repo file: `quoted_text` of `"}"`, `";"`, `"import"`, and `"  return  "` each returned `{"status":"grounded"}`. Every one of those substrings appears in essentially every source file in the repo, so the gate is satisfiable without reading the file at all.

WHY IT MATTERS: this makes `grounded` carry close to zero evidential weight while the report and the remediator both treat it as the confirmed state. `synthesis.ts:465` tells the reader that ungrounded findings are "not confirmed — treat them with skepticism", which by contrast asserts that grounded findings ARE confirmed; and as in DR-001, `grounded` suppresses the remediator's VERIFY-BEFORE-FIX bullet. A weak or adversarial worker that emits plausible-sounding findings with a `}` quote gets them all marked confirmed and fixed unverified. Note this defeats the gate in the *opposite* direction from the one the design worried about: the docstring reasons carefully about false NEGATIVES (line shifts must not false-fail a valid quote) and not at all about false POSITIVES.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: require the cited span to be evidence rather than merely present. Concretely: enforce a minimum normalized length (a span shorter than ~30 normalized chars or fewer than ~3 tokens grounds nothing), require the match to be reasonably unique in the file (reject a needle occurring more than N times), and — since `line_start`/`line_end` are already validated against `file_coverage` — require the matched offset to fall inside the finding's own cited span rather than anywhere in the file. All three are mechanical and cheap, and they keep the deliberate whitespace/CRLF tolerance intact.

- Details: Do not grade your own homework — anything important gets an independent adversarial check that is allowed to refuse — is one of the project's headline convictions, and independence is the property the entire adversarial layer's value rests on. It is currently guaranteed by asking the host politely. renderIndependentReviewerDirective (src/audit/orchestrator/designReviewPrompt.ts:202-219) emits prose: the host MUST dispatch this review to a fresh, independent sub-agent that did not author the work, and must NOT perform the review inline. Nothing verifies it happened. There is no reviewer identity on a review result, no session or provider provenance recorded for a review, and no refusal path when the reviewing context is the authoring context — searching reviewer_id / reviewed_by / author_session across src/audit, src/remediate and src/shared finds provenance fields for charters, capabilities and analyzers, but none for who performed a review. The test makes the gap unusually visible because it tests the request rather than the outcome: tests/audit/mandatory-independent-critic.test.ts:28-46 asserts the prompt STRING matches /Independent review — MANDATORY/ and /MUST dispatch/. A green suite proves the tool asked, not that anyone complied. The FreshSessionProvider contract (src/shared/providers/types.ts:143-153) offers launch and nothing about identity, so even the provider layer cannot express 'this reviewer differs from that author'. The degraded branch is honest about running inline when the host reports it cannot dispatch (:217-219), but that capability flag is host-asserted too, so a host can select its own degradation. This is A3 inverted at the one place it matters most: everywhere else audit-tools refuses to trust the host (a finding must carry a verbatim span the tool re-reads from disk, and the confirmed bit is the tool's re-check, never the model's word), and that pattern is absent one layer up where the question shifts from 'is this finding real' to 'was this judgment independent'. A capable host complies; a weak one self-reviews and produces output indistinguishable from the real thing — precisely the failure the North Star exists to rule out. Recommendation: have the dispatch substrate, not the prompt, stamp each review artifact with the identity of the session/provider that produced it, and have ingest refuse or downgrade to a surfaced self_reviewed verdict — exactly as ungrounded is surfaced — when a review's producer identity matches the authoring producer or is absent. The parallel-perspective fan-out already writes each reviewer's findings to a separate file, so the seam where identity could be stamped already exists. Independence then degrades visibly instead of silently, which is all the North Star requires.

All of these problems are artifacts of the wrong seam: lint-staged has solved staged-snapshot materialization including the stash edge cases, and lefthook or husky install real git hooks from tracked, versioned config so the gate binds for every client and every clone. The coupling has also hardened into the suite: tests/shared/shared-core-invariants.test.ts (INV-shared-core-16) asserts the hook exists AND that settings.json registers it as a PreToolUse hook, so the host dependency is now a tested contract. Recommendation: move the gate body into a tracked .githooks/pre-commit wired via core.hooksPath (set in postinstall) or lefthook, invoke the staged-snapshot check through lint-staged, split the remaining checks into one module per check behind a small declarative registry that check:guard-reach reconciles against (the shape scripts/guard-reach-data.mjs and src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts already prove), and delete shell-split.mjs and the bypass-token regex entirely — a real pre-commit hook never parses a command line.

StateStore.mutate (src/remediate/state/store.ts:301-314) is the safe shape: read-modify-write entirely inside the lock (src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts:104-117). StateStore.saveState (:322-327) delegates to replace, which takes the lock and writes the caller's whole object WITHOUT reading first (lockedJsonStore.ts:118-126), so the lock prevents a torn file but not a lost update: a caller that read at T0 and calls saveState at T1 silently discards everything a peer persisted in between. Worse, the guarantee is contradicted by design intent: A9 wants arbitrary cooperative peers advancing one run, making 'no concurrent writer exists' false by construction. The phase:main mutex (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:5475) is the only thing holding this together and does not cover everything that persists — countStep's closure ends in saveState (:5389-5395) and is invoked at :5463 before the mutex is acquired, writing a full state snapshot derived from a lockless read at :5345. The asymmetry is the design signal: the audit half solved this properly, claiming a bundle-mutation node, executing unlocked under a heartbeat, and re-validating ownership before persisting (src/audit/cli/auditStep.ts:243-258). This is one-core-two-draws breaking down in the most safety-critical substrate in the repo. Supporting detail: the signal that would let a de-claimed writer abandon its work exists and is dead — onRevoked (src/shared/quota/claimLease.ts:57-58,86-89) has zero production callers, only a test. Recommendation: delete saveState rather than document it, so the unsafe shape is unavailable; the recovery case it exists for (a corrupt on-disk state must not block recovery) is expressible as a mutate whose function ignores current, keeping the lock-held read-modify-write frame. Then wire onRevoked so a revoked claim abandons instead of finishing, and hoist the audit half's ownership re-validation into the shared core so both draws inherit it.

INFERRED CONTRACT: the names and the surrounding docs all assert confinement — `enforceWriteScope`, `writeScopeViolations`, "Worker edited files outside its declared write scope" (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/writeScope.ts:58), and CLAUDE.md lists "write-scope enforcement" among the properties that must be guaranteed by the tool rather than by the host remembering.

- Severity: high
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/remediate/steps/dispatch/writeScope.ts`, `src/remediate/steps/dispatch/common.ts`, `src/remediate/steps/dispatch/acceptNode.ts`, `src/remediate/dispatch/ownershipRegistry.ts`
- Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: the names and the surrounding docs all assert confinement — `enforceWriteScope`, `writeScopeViolations`, "Worker edited files outside its declared write scope" (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/writeScope.ts:58), and CLAUDE.md lists "write-scope enforcement" among the properties that must be guaranteed by the tool rather than by the host remembering. A reader reasonably infers: a worker's edits are restricted to its declared `write_paths`.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the effective rule is `blocked ⟺ ∃ edited file f ∉ declaredScope(thisBlock) ∧ f ∈ declaredScope(someSiblingBlock)`. Any out-of-declared edit to a file NO SIBLING declared is granted and widens the node's effective scope (`adjudicateWriteScope`, writeScope.ts:106-147, and its own docstring at :97-99). Verified by running the shipped code with an edit set of `{src/declared.ts, src/UNDECLARED.ts, package.json, .github/workflows/release.yml}` against a block declaring only `src/declared.ts`:
  single block                          → `{blocked: false}`
  two blocks, sibling declares src/other.ts → `{blocked: false}`
  sibling declares package.json             → `{blocked: true}` (seam conflict)
  empty registry                            → `{blocked: false}`
So on a single-block wave the gate cannot block on scope at all: a worker may rewrite `package.json`, a release workflow, or any other file in the tree and the accept passes. The same holds when the dispatch plan cannot be read and `allBlockScopes` degrades to `[]` (documented as "a sound no-op, never a skip" at acceptNode.ts:86-87).

ASSESSMENT: the grant behaviour is deliberate and test-pinned (tests/remediate/dispatch-evidence-and-writescope.test.ts:587-591, "GRANTS an edit to an UNOWNED file no sibling declared") — the finding is not that the code disagrees with its own tests, but that the CONTRACT the rest of the system advertises is confinement while the mechanism provides only collision arbitration. Two real consequences: (a) `write_paths` is not a safety boundary, so nothing mechanically prevents a remediation worker from editing infrastructure it was never scoped to; (b) the declared scope is load-bearing elsewhere (verification commands, region ownership scheduling) yet is silently mutable by the worker's actual behaviour.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: separate the two questions rather than conflating them in one predicate. Keep seam arbitration as-is, but add a genuine confinement boundary that does not depend on sibling declarations — e.g. a per-run "never writable" set (lockfiles, CI workflows, `package.json`, release scripts) that blocks regardless of ownership, and require an explicit widening record (not a silent grant) when a node edits outside its declared scope. If unowned-grant must stay the default, rename the mechanism to what it does (`adjudicateCrossBlockOwnership`) so no future reader infers a confinement guarantee that was never there.

- Confidence: high

- Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: the project's central invariant — "Auditor-agnostic robustness — enforce in tooling, never host discretion... Any place the workflow only works because a capable host folded in guidance... is a latent failure mode" (CLAUDE.md). For remediation the two tool-owned guarantees are the write-scope gate and the merge-state gate that distinguishes edits that actually LANDED from a worker that merely self-reported `resolved` ("OBL-DS-06: never trust the worker's self report", src/remediate/steps/dispatch/acceptNode.ts:777-781).

COUNTEREXAMPLE: both gates are structurally unreachable on the dispatch paths that run nodes in the operator's real checkout instead of a per-node worktree. The enforcement chain is `executeNodeInWorktree` → `acceptNodeWorktree` → `enforceAcceptWriteScope` (acceptNode.ts:565-576), and the ground truth it consumes is a per-node branch diff (`git diff --name-only HEAD...<branch>`, common.ts:166-170). With no worktree there is no branch, so there is no diff and no gate. The codebase states this outright in two places: "The write-scope gate itself is NOT applied here: it runs at ACCEPT time... A missing branch means the interim main-tree path was used (no per-worker diff): nothing to collect" (marshal.ts:1294-1300), and "the interim main-tree path writes none, so the merge-state gate is inert there" (acceptNode.ts:782). The affected paths include the non-rolling host fan-out `dispatch_implement` and `implement_rolling_sequential` (src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts, the `dispatch_implement` and sequential branches), where the surviving controls are prompt text (implementPrompt.ts) and the worker's self-reported `amended_files` (marshal.ts:891-900) — i.e. precisely the "host remembering" and "worker self-report" that the invariant forbids.

WHY THIS IS A COVERAGE GAP RATHER THAN A BUG: each gate is correct where it runs; what is missing is that the guarantee is advertised as a property of remediation while being a property of *one dispatch topology*. Nothing marks the main-tree paths as unsafe to an operator, and nothing prevents a future path from inheriting the same hole. The repo's own memory note "a script in no gate is not a gate" is the same failure shape one level up.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: make the enforcement unconditional on topology. Either (a) require worktree isolation for every implement dispatch and delete the main-tree paths (consistent with the project's stated preference for deleting legacy paths over keeping a lighter half-measure), or (b) give the main-tree path an equivalent tool-owned ground truth — snapshot `git status --porcelain`/a tree hash before dispatch and diff after, then run the SAME `adjudicateWriteScope` and merge-state logic against that edit set. Whichever is chosen, add a contract test asserting that every dispatch path reaching a provider also reaches a write-scope adjudication, so a third path cannot be added gate-free.

### ARC-479f5151-2 — Acyclicity of the DAG-is-truth artifact graph is preserved by prose arguments and by omitting a real edge, and LLM-authored nodes sit under byte-exact staleness

The load-bearing axiom is that artifacts are continuity and the dependency DAG is truth — staleness propagates along one explicit acyclic relation, never ad-hoc checks.

- Severity: high
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/audit/orchestrator/dependencyMap.ts`, `src/audit/io/artifacts.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/staleness.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/artifactMetadata.ts` +1 more
- Details: The load-bearing axiom is that artifacts are continuity and the dependency DAG is truth — staleness propagates along one explicit acyclic relation, never ad-hoc checks. src/audit/orchestrator/dependencyMap.ts implements it well in one respect worth crediting: ARTIFACT_DEPENDS_ON_MAP is the single hand-authored adjacency and the forward view is computed by invertDependencyMap, so there is exactly one hand-authored adjacency representation and everything else is computed from it. But the relation the domain actually has is not acyclic, and the map keeps it acyclic by argument rather than by construction. Across 25 nodes there are five separate acyclicity arguments in comments (lines 48, 108, 141, 164, 167), three of the same form: no cycle, because the executor writes X AND Y in one advanceAudit call, dependency-first. That is not the absence of a cycle — it is a cycle whose two endpoints are written atomically, so the ordering inside the pair never has to be resolved. And one comment concedes the graph is missing a real edge to stay acyclic: access-memory is a genuine input to packet composition, but the dependency threads in at the dispatch code level rather than as a DAG edge, to avoid a coverage-to-results-to-access_memory-to-coverage cycle (line 167). So the artifact declared to be truth is knowingly incomplete, and the omitted edge is exactly the kind of feedback the audit pipeline is built on. A second, related strain: several interior nodes are LLM-authored (charter_register.json is produced by the LLM charter pass and is upstream of both charter_clarification.json and systemic_challenge.json) while the staleness algebra is exact content-hash equality, so any source edit re-stales the register, whose regenerated bytes will differ even when its meaning does not, cascading two further expensive LLM passes. The repo already knows this hazard for deterministic extractors — the stable-array-order rule exists precisely because incidental ordering silently churns a content hash and cascades phantom staleness — but for a non-deterministic producer that mitigation is unavailable, so the assumption that hash inequality implies downstream invalidity is unsound on exactly the nodes where re-running is most expensive. Recommendation, the standard clean-sheet formulation for both strains: make the atomic write-set a first-class node. Executors already declare their write-sets as data — tests/audit/seam-dependency-map-executor-writeset-parity.test.ts recovers them by reading executor module source text to cross-check the map — so the ingredients exist. Group artifacts by the write-set that produces them, define dependencies between groups, and acyclicity becomes a property the tool checks on the condensation (an SCC condensation is always a DAG) instead of five prose arguments and one deliberately-missing edge; that also gives the omitted access-memory dependency a legal home. Separately, mark LLM-authored nodes with a semantic rather than byte freshness key so a regenerated-but-equivalent artifact does not fan out three LLM re-runs.

The project persists run state as JSON files guarded by a hand-built advisory-lock stack: src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts (293 lines), src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts, claimRegistry.ts, claimLease.ts, reservationLedger.ts, quota/state.ts, src/remediate/state/store.ts, src/remediate/contractPipeline/artifactStore.ts, plus temp-then-rename atomic writes in src/shared/io/json.ts and staleness bookkeeping in staleness.ts / artifactMetadata.ts — 3,946 lines across those files alone.

- Grounding: grounded

- Details: The project persists run state as JSON files guarded by a hand-built advisory-lock stack: src/shared/quota/fileLock.ts (293 lines), src/shared/io/lockedJsonStore.ts, claimRegistry.ts, claimLease.ts, reservationLedger.ts, quota/state.ts, src/remediate/state/store.ts, src/remediate/contractPipeline/artifactStore.ts, plus temp-then-rename atomic writes in src/shared/io/json.ts and staleness bookkeeping in staleness.ts / artifactMetadata.ts — 3,946 lines across those files alone. Nearly all of the hardest logic exists for ONE reason: a filesystem lock cannot detect a dead holder. That single gap is why the code needs STALE_LOCK_MS (30s), owner tokens, mtime heartbeats, a .steal sidecar claim to serialize stale removal, token-checked reclaim, and Windows EPERM/EACCES retry paths. The file's own comments record that the first implementation admitted a real double-hold race (two stealers both believing they held the lock), fixed by adding the sidecar — precisely the class of bug a mature library has already absorbed. The 30s window then leaks upward as a standing design tension: src/audit/cli/auditStep.ts:121, src/remediate/steps/nextStep.ts:2632, src/shared/dispatch/admissionLoop.ts:374 and src/remediate/state/store.ts:231 all reason explicitly about heartbeating inside or timing out under STALE_LOCK_MS. An embedded SQL engine makes the apparatus unnecessary: a BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction is kernel-mediated per connection, so a crashed peer's lock releases IMMEDIATELY rather than after a 30-second heuristic — no stale window, no heartbeat, no steal race, no token protocol; a UNIQUE constraint on node_id expresses claim exclusivity directly; and WAL mode gives concurrent readers with a single writer for free. This matters most for the direction actively being built: spec/multi-ide-concurrent-runs-design.md targets an arbitrary number of agents cooperating on ONE shared run with ClaimRegistry plus withFileLock as its stated substrate — i.e. a genuine multi-process transactional workload implemented on advisory file locks — and the three gaps that spec enumerates (a coarse lock serializing peers, no task-level claiming, a single clobbered step slot) are all standard SQL problems. Recommendation: adopt node:sqlite (built into Node, zero dependencies, no native build — strictly better than the project's own pure-JS-so-OS-agnostic bar) for run state, claims and the artifact/staleness ledger, keeping the JSON/markdown deliverables as rendered exports; the cost is raising the engines.node floor above 20. Confidence is medium and one genuine disagreement is worth recording rather than resolving: the adversarial perspective independently judged fileLock.ts unusually careful and correct (exclusive wx create with owner token, bounded backoff clamped to time-remaining, a live-holder heartbeat at one third of the stale window, stale-steal serialized through its own sidecar with a token re-check before unlink, and timeout as a THROW rather than proceeding unlocked). Both readings are compatible — this is a careful implementation of a mechanism that may not need to exist — but a migration trades a well-understood, well-tested substrate for a new one, and DR-010 is a lost-update defect that should be fixed on the current substrate regardless of this decision. Note the project already tolerates SQLite in its environment: src/shared/quota/antigravityQuotaSource.ts shells out to the sqlite3 CLI to read a host token.

### ARC-1ec7c91d-2 — Anchor argument policy does not confine inspection to the audited repo: `git --git-dir=`, `--work-tree=`, and absolute search positionals are admitted

INFERRED CONTRACT: the anchor pass inspects the repository under audit.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts`, `src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts`
- Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: the anchor pass inspects the repository under audit. The runner is handed `cwd = repoRoot` (src/audit/validation/anchorGrounding.ts:178), the argument policy is default-deny and curated per executable specifically so "positionals (search patterns / file paths) are allowed — they name what to inspect, not code to run" (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts:18-20), and `git` gets extra treatment because its options can escape read-only inspection (`GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS`, :195-203).

COUNTEREXAMPLE: nothing confines *which files* are inspected. The permitted positional is any string, including an absolute path outside the repo, and git's cwd-redirecting options are not in the refused set. Verified by running the shipped code:
  `["git","--git-dir=C:/other/.git","log"]`   → allowed: true
  `["git","--work-tree=C:/other","status"]`   → allowed: true
  `["grep","-r","secret","C:/Users"]`         → allowed: true
  `["rg","--hidden","AKIA","C:/Users/ethan"]`  → allowed: true
(`["git","-C","dir","log"]` is refused, but only incidentally — the separated `dir` positional is mistaken for the subcommand and fails the read-only-subcommand check, so the protection is an accident of the parser rather than a rule. The `--git-dir=`/`--work-tree=` attached forms sail through.)

WHY IT MATTERS: combined with model-authored `confirm_if` (DR-001), each anchor is a one-bit read oracle over an arbitrary filesystem path: `rg --hidden 'AKIA[A-Z0-9]{16}' C:/Users/<user>` with `confirm_if: {kind: "output_includes", text: "AKIA"}` returns confirmed exactly when such a string exists, and the persisted evidence line records the command that was run (`anchorEvidenceLine`, anchorGrounding.ts:240). The `--hidden`/`--no-ignore` flags are on the allowlist, so dotfile directories are in reach. This is not bulk exfiltration — only the summary line, not the captured output, is folded into `finding.evidence` (mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:619-623) — but it is an unbounded read predicate over the host filesystem authored by the model, which is a strictly larger boundary than "inspect the audited repo".

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: containment-check every positional the same way DR-003 recommends for cited paths — reject any argument that `resolveWithinRoot(repoRoot, arg)` does not place inside the audited root (with an allowance for pattern arguments, which are distinguishable by position for each allowlisted tool). Add `--git-dir`, `--work-tree`, and `--namespace` (attached and separated forms) to `GIT_REFUSED_OPTIONS`, and make the read-only-subcommand check positional-aware rather than "first token not starting with `-`".

### ARC-305e7ec5 — Closing-action authority is flat across a steep blast-radius gradient: one pre_authorized bit waives the preview for publish exactly as for commit

The remediate half ends by taking a real action on the user's world.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/remediate/phases/close.ts`, `src/remediate/state/closingActions.ts`, `src/remediate/state/types.ts`, `src/remediate/review/autonomousGate.ts`
- Details: The remediate half ends by taking a real action on the user's world. The four actions — commit, push, open-pr, publish (src/remediate/state/closingActions.ts:2-5) — span an enormous range of reversibility: a local commit is trivially undone; publishing to a package registry is public, immediate, and effectively immutable. The authority model does not reflect that range. All four are in PREVIEW_ACTIONS and get a confirmation preview by default, which is right (src/remediate/phases/close.ts:717), but checkClosingPreview short-circuits on a single boolean BEFORE it looks at which action is involved — pre_authorized === true returns immediately (close.ts:730) and only then does it consult PREVIEW_ACTIONS. One bit therefore waives the preview for publish on exactly the same terms as for commit. The deeper mismatch is temporal rather than merely granular: per the product's own flow the operator sets the closing action and pre-authorization UP FRONT, before planning and implementation run, so consent is granted before the artifact it authorizes exists. At confirmation time the operator does not know the file list, the diff, the version that will be published, or whether the review gate auto-approved anything. For a local commit that is a reasonable trade for autonomy; for an irreversible public release it means the one human checkpoint occurs at the point of minimum information. Note also that custom_command proceeds without preview by construction (close.ts:731 — it is not in PREVIEW_ACTIONS) and is argv-spawned at close.ts:845-846. Credit where due, because it shows the project already knows how to do this: the autonomous review gate is a model of the right shape — a fail-closed CLOSED enumeration of four provably-safe change kinds, explicitly refusing any severity/cost shortcut, with anything unclassifiable excluded by default (src/remediate/review/autonomousGate.ts:26-70). That rigor stops at the door where the blast radius is largest. Recommendation: make the authority per-action rather than per-run and tier it by reversibility — pre_authorized becomes a set of authorized actions rather than a boolean, and the irreversible tier (publish, and arguably push to a protected branch) requires confirmation AT EXECUTION with the actual preview attached, regardless of up-front pre-authorization; the preview material is already computed by collectStagingFiles and generateCommitMessage. Reversible actions keep today's frictionless autonomy.
- Evidence: 2 items (top: "runtime:flow:flow:host:remediation-state-machine: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### PRF-7c1a1951 — Every artifact-bundle load re-hashes audit-tools' own 10.3 MB / 2,109-file install to recompute a value that cannot change during a run

loadArtifactBundle unconditionally calls buildToolingManifest() (src/audit/io/artifacts.ts:333).

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: performance
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/audit/io/toolingManifest.ts`, `src/audit/io/artifacts.ts`, `src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts`
- Details: loadArtifactBundle unconditionally calls buildToolingManifest() (src/audit/io/artifacts.ts:333). That function recursively walks and reads EVERY byte of six inputs — audit-code.mjs, wrapper/audit-code-wrapper-lib.mjs, package.json, dist/, schemas/, skills/audit-code — serially (one await readFile per file inside a for loop, src/audit/io/toolingManifest.ts:74-87) and folds them into one sha256. Measured on this tree: 2,109 files / 10,317,315 bytes for dist alone, 282-369 ms per call (first call 369 ms, warm repeat 282 ms) against the audit-tools dist actually on disk. For scale, the ENTIRE rest of the load->hash->persist cycle over the live 8.7 MB artifact set measures 122 ms total (parse 27 ms + hash-every-artifact 62 ms + persist-every-artifact 33 ms), so the tool spends 2.5-3x more time hashing ITSELF than handling all of the audit state it exists to manage. The value is a fixed identity of the installed implementation: it cannot change while a run is in flight (a mid-run rebuild of the tool being audited is not a supported state — the artifact even records it as implementation_hash + package_version). Yet loadArtifactBundle has 29 call sites, and nextStepHelpers.ts alone re-loads the whole bundle at 12 separate 'transition' points, so one folded next-step invocation can pay it a dozen times. Two better mechanisms, either of which removes the cost entirely: (a) emit the implementation hash at BUILD time into a generated dist module (one read instead of 2,109 — the identity is a property of the build, not of run-time disk state), or (b) at minimum memoize per process. (b) is a two-line change; (a) is the categorically right one because it also makes the identity stable across concurrent readers and machines instead of re-deriving it from whatever bytes happen to be on disk.

### OPR-7957ede5 — Every CI job rebuilds dist from scratch and the test matrix shards by file count rather than duration, so the CI critical path is ~1.7x its achievable floor

Two independent inefficiencies in the same matrix, both measured from the repo's own publish-ci profile record.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: operability
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `.github/workflows/publish-package.yml`, `.github/workflows/audit-code-test-suite.yml`
- Details: Two independent inefficiencies in the same matrix, both measured from the repo's own publish-ci profile record. (a) Redundant build: actions/upload-artifact appears only for npm debug logs and download-artifact appears nowhere, so dist/ is never shared between jobs - each of the four test shards runs its own Build (9-11 s each), the publish job builds again, and the gate job builds a third time inside verify:checks, totalling 51 s of identical compilation across 5 occurrences in one run. audit-code-test-suite.yml has the same per-job Build across its 8-job (2 Node lines x 4 shards) matrix, so a push to main compiles the same commit eight times. setup-node's cache: npm already makes install cheap (3 s typical), which is exactly the pattern build is missing: build once, upload dist, download in every consumer job. (b) Duration-blind sharding: vitest --shard partitions by FILE, not by measured duration, and the run's shard times are 205 s / 127 s / 92 s / 60 s. The matrix wall is set by the slowest shard, so the test critical path is 205 s where a duration-balanced split of the same 484 s of work would be ~121 s - a 41% reduction available with no extra runners. Deriving the split from recorded per-file durations (the vitest-history.ndjson profile already collected in .audit-tools-profile) or raising the shard count for finer granularity recovers it. Together these take ~85 s off the critical path and ~40 s of billed compute per run, on a pipeline that currently measures 1,459 s wall.

### PRF-1e62173d — Extraction opens every source file four to five times and every per-file loop is serial, while the repo's own bounded-concurrency helper is used zero times in the extraction path and its single parallel site is unbounded

There is no shared content pass.

- Details: There is no shared content pass. fsIntake reads each file in full and throws the bytes away — maybeHashFile does `const content = await readFile(path); return hashContent(content)` (src/audit/extractors/fsIntake.ts:46-53) and the returned manifest carries only {path, size_bytes, hash}. Then graph.ts re-reads every in-scope file into its own function-local fileContents map (src/audit/extractors/graph.ts:507-531) and discards it on return (:543); the per-language analyzers re-read their subsets independently (python.ts:109-112, html.ts:80-83, css.ts:94-97, and typescript.ts:399-400 lets ts.createProgram read them a fourth time); and commentDecomposition re-reads every included file plus every doc file (src/audit/extractors/commentDecomposition.ts:270-271 and :345-346) even though it exposes a readFileText injection seam the only production caller leaves undefined. So one .ts file is opened 4x in-process per extraction and a scanned .md 5x, over 1,210 included files / 13.3 MB measured here. The shape is also serial almost everywhere: the intake walk awaits readdir/stat/hash per entry (fsIntake.ts:77-105) and I measured the same file set at 139 ms read serially vs 39 ms concurrently (3.6x); commentDecomposition, python, html and css all await inside a for-over-files; and the analyzers themselves run strictly one-after-another in a registry for loop (src/audit/orchestrator/graphEnrichmentExecutor.ts:239-256) despite being independent, so a polyglot repo pays the SUM of analyzer times rather than the max. Meanwhile src/shared/concurrency.ts (mapWithConcurrency) exists and is called from exactly two post-ingest sites and zero extraction sites, and the one place extraction IS concurrent — graph.ts:507 — is an unbounded Promise.all over every in-scope file, i.e. the only parallel site is the one that should have a cap. The better arrangement is one bounded read pass that hashes and hands the same buffer to the graph, the analyzers and the comment pass, with mapWithConcurrency as the single primitive: it removes 3 of the 4 passes, replaces the 3.6x-slower serial walk, bounds the fd fan-out, and lets independent analyzers overlap. Worth noting what the incremental tier does and does not cover: the per-file content-keyed reuse in graph.ts:911-916 (via graph_edge_cache) is the right pattern but sits BEHIND the read pass (a 100% cache hit still reads every file) and the analyzer tier has no equivalent — typescript.ts:100 explicitly forces incremental:false/composite:false, so the measured 7.4 s graph-enrichment step rebuilds the whole program whenever it runs at all.

The core of this product is graph work — import/call/co-change edges, connected components, clustering under size ceilings, cycle detection, topological tiering, transitive staleness propagation — and every algorithm is written from scratch with no graph dependency of any kind.

- Details: The core of this product is graph work — import/call/co-change edges, connected components, clustering under size ceilings, cycle detection, topological tiering, transitive staleness propagation — and every algorithm is written from scratch with no graph dependency of any kind. The duplication is measurable. Union-find appears FOUR times: src/audit/orchestrator/unionFind.ts (the named module), a private class in src/shared/decompose/consensus.ts:121-163, inline find/union closures in src/remediate/contractPipeline/cyclicSeamResolution.ts:110-123, and an array-indexed variant in src/audit/orchestrator/partitionTaskGraph.ts:60-71. Cycle detection appears three times in two different styles: DFS-with-rotation-canonical-dedupe in src/audit/extractors/graphSignals.ts:169-212, and three-colour DFS twice, in src/shared/types/obligationLedger.ts:27-63 and src/remediate/validation/contractPipeline.ts:664-698. Two separate hand-rolled bounded-concurrency primitives exist as well — src/shared/concurrency.ts (mapWithConcurrency) and src/shared/quota/slidingWindow.ts (runSlidingWindow) — and the second has no production caller at all, reachable only through re-exports and its own tests, so it is a live instance of the tested-but-unwired class the project tracks manually; it also recurses per completed task, growing a promise chain rather than looping. This is not primarily a correctness complaint — the implementations look careful — it is that the project pays maintenance on a private algorithms library while its own principles say to single-source common logic and prefer extraction over parallel copies. Recommendation: adopt graphology with graphology-components, graphology-dag and graphology-traversal (pure JS, no native build, actively maintained) for components, cycle detection and topological ordering; replace the two concurrency primitives with one, or at minimum delete runSlidingWindow. Retain only the genuinely domain-specific passes — the size-ceiling clustering and the consensus co-association — on top of the library's data structures. Note the interaction with DR-023: a library-provided SCC condensation is exactly the mechanism that would turn the dependency map's five prose acyclicity arguments into a checked property.

- Details: TRUST BOUNDARY: `finding.affected_files[].path` is worker output — untrusted data crossing from the LLM into the tool. Every other consumer of a model-supplied path in this codebase routes it through the single containment guard `resolveWithinRoot` (src/shared/io/pathContainment.ts), whose docstring records that this check was reimplemented five times and that "this is the class where that is a security property, not a style preference".

COUNTEREXAMPLE: the grounding verifier does not use it. `verifyFindingGrounding` resolves the cited path as `const absolutePath = isAbsolute(loc.path) ? loc.path : join(repoRoot, loc.path)` (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:182) — an absolute path is passed through verbatim, and a relative path is `join`ed with no `..` rejection. Verified by running the shipped code: a finding citing `{path: "../../Windows/win.ini", quoted_text: "for 16-bit app support"}` with `repoRoot` set to this repository returned `{"status":"grounded"}`. So the `grounded` bit does not even assert that the cited location is in the repository under audit.

REACHABILITY: this is not filtered upstream. The result validator deliberately keeps such a finding: an `affected_files[].path` outside the declared assigned coverage is pushed as `severity: "warning"` with the message "In-scope findings are retained; this entry is informational only" (src/audit/validation/auditResults.ts:962-974, INV-09/FRIC-010). The path is never containment-checked before it reaches the grounding pass. Note the asymmetry with the sibling normalizer in the same shared module, `normalizeRepoPath` (findingGrounding.ts:46), which is careful about path shape but is used for corpus membership, not for the filesystem read.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: run the cited path through `resolveWithinRoot(repoRoot, loc.path)` before reading it, and classify a non-contained path as `ungrounded` with an explicit reason ("cited path escapes the audited root") rather than reading it. This is a two-line change at findingGrounding.ts:182 and makes the grounding verdict mean what the report claims it means. Consider also promoting the out-of-scope `affected_files` path from warning to a grounding-disqualifier, so the retained-but-informational entry cannot silently become a confirmed one.

### COR-a75a10c1 — Louvain aggregation undercounts self-loop degree, breaking the documented degree-preservation invariant

aggregate() claims each super-node's degree equals the total degree of its members, but buildAdjacency counts the diagonal (self-loop) ONCE in a node's degree.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: correctness
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:73–107`, `src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:223–232`, `src/shared/decompose/modularity.ts:52–53`
- Details: aggregate() claims each super-node's degree equals the total degree of its members, but buildAdjacency counts the diagonal (self-loop) ONCE in a node's degree. An intra-community pair edge of weight w contributes 2w to member degrees at level N but only w to the super-node's degree (and only w to 2m) at level N+1, so every aggregated level optimizes a distorted modularity: communities with intra mass look 'lighter' than they are, biasing coarse levels toward over-merging. For the multilevel method to be exact, a self-loop must contribute twice its weight to the node's degree (standard Louvain convention).

### ARC-1b6df28c — npm install rewrites the consuming repo's .gitignore and shells out to gh to guess repository visibility

Installing the package mutates the user's repository.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/io/gitignoreArtifacts.ts`, `scripts/postinstall.mjs`, `README.md`
- Details: Installing the package mutates the user's repository. scripts/postinstall.mjs:31 calls manageArtifactGitignore(), which resolves INIT_CWD as the consuming repo root and writes a marker-delimited managed block into that repo's .gitignore (src/shared/io/gitignoreArtifacts.ts:143-199). To decide the block's contents it runs a four-tier visibility-authority chain: an environment variable, then a committed .audit-tools-visibility marker file, then gh repo view --json isPrivate — a GitHub CLI subprocess during npm install (:202-232). That is 351 lines plus a network-capable shell-out, and the decision it buys is whether one output file is tracked by default. Three things make this a poor trade regardless of how carefully it degrades. A postinstall script writing to a file the user's VCS tracks is surprising in a way no amount of idempotency fixes — it will show up as an unexplained diff. Inferring intent from repository visibility is a guess about a policy question the user is better placed to answer, and a wrong guess in the private-to-public direction is exactly the leak the feature exists to prevent. And an npm install that invokes gh will behave differently in CI, in a container, and offline, for reasons unrelated to installing a package. Recommendation: delete the inference. Always ignore the runtime tree (.audit-tools/audit/, .audit-tools/remediation/) since it is machine state nobody wants committed, never touch .gitignore for the deliverables, and document in the README the one line a user adds if they want audit-report.md tracked. That removes 351 lines, a subprocess, an environment variable, a marker file, and a class of surprise, and hands a policy decision back to the person who owns it. Note DR-020: this file also runs on every consumer machine and is outside every tsconfig.

- Files: `src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPacketGraphContext.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/reviewPackets.ts`, `src/audit/cli/dispatch/packetFilter.ts`, `src/audit/cli/dispatch.ts` +1 more
- Details: buildReviewPackets does its graph work correctly ONCE and then undoes that discipline per packet. collectGraphEdges (reviewPackets.ts:475), buildPlanningGraphEdges (:478) and mergeGraphConnectedGroups (:489) each run a single time over the whole edge set, but the emit loop (:500-518) then calls buildPacket PER PACKET, and every buildPacket calls buildPacketGraphContext (:390), which iterates the ENTIRE planningGraphEdges array (reviewPacketGraphContext.ts:81) and, via packetEntrypoints (:120), filters the entire graphs.routes array as well. So the payload build is O(packets x edges) sitting behind a clustering pass that is already O(edges). Measured against this repo's own artifacts (collectGraphEdges returns 6,614 concrete edges from the 3.37 MB graph_bundle.json): buildReviewPackets over 141 synthetic tasks on real repo paths costs 861 ms, over 468 tasks 2,335 ms; the identical call with no graphBundle supplied costs 32 ms and 35 ms, so ~98.5% of packetization time is the per-packet graph payload. I prototyped the fix and measured it: building one endpoint->edges adjacency index ONCE and visiting only the edges incident to each packet's own files produces byte-identical internal/boundary counts (11,724 both ways) and drops the kernel from 90.6 ms to 3.6 ms for 100 packets over the 6,614 edges - 25x. The module already exports exactly this primitive, buildGraphDegreeIndex (reviewPacketGraph.ts:24), and buildPacketGraphContext does not use it. Second, independent half: orderTasksForPacketReview (reviewPackets.ts:599) is `buildReviewPackets(tasks, options).flatMap(...)` (:604) - it pays the whole per-packet payload and then reduces the packets to a task-id list. That ordering cannot depend on the payload: makeComparePackets (:158) sorts on priority -> continuity -> task count -> packet_id and reads no graph field. It is called from dispatch.ts:376 and from buildPendingAuditTasks (packetFilter.ts:59, :73), whose five callers are dispatch.ts:272, mergeAndIngestCommand.ts:958, reviewRun.ts:135, nextStepHelpers.ts:2434 and nextStepHelpers.ts:2640 - and the last two need no ordering at all (2434 consumes only {task_id, token_estimate}; 2640, the unconditional next-step preamble, consumes only the file_line_counts key set). The code comments at packetFilter.ts:69-72 and dispatch.ts:369-371 already record that the order is re-derived downstream, so the discarded work is known; what was never priced is that discarding a packet still costs a full edge sweep. Three changes, all local: index the edges once, give the pending-set-only callers derivePendingTaskPartition directly, and let the order-only path cluster without building packet payloads.
