### ARC-7b11d8bc — Quota and rate-limit classification depends on regex-matching vendor PROSE, because nine of ten providers are CLI subprocesses with no structured error channel

The load-bearing assumption behind the whole quota subsystem is that a vendor CLI's human-readable stderr is a stable machine interface.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/shared/quota/errorParsing.ts`, `src/shared/providers/providerFactory.ts`, `src/shared/providers/openAiCompatibleProvider.ts`, `src/shared/types/sessionConfig.ts` +1 more
- Details: The load-bearing assumption behind the whole quota subsystem is that a vendor CLI's human-readable stderr is a stable machine interface. src/shared/quota/errorParsing.ts (425 lines) classifies dispatch failures by matching English against captured output: RATE_LIMIT_PATTERNS, USAGE_LIMIT_PATTERNS, CREDIT_EXHAUSTION_PATTERNS, and a RESET_INDICATOR_PATTERN that vetoes a credit match when the prose sounds transient. The comments are candid that this is load-bearing and fragile — the veto exists because permanently sinking a pool that would have recovered is worse than the bug it fixes. None of it would be necessary with a structured channel: HTTP gives 429 plus Retry-After as a standard, and every vendor emits machine-readable error codes in the response body. The reason it is necessary is architectural and worth naming as such: of the ten entries in PROVIDER_NAMES, nine dispatch by spawning a subprocess (claude, codex, opencode, agy, plus the template-driven vscode-task/antigravity/worker-command/subprocess-template and the proxied claude-worker), and exactly one — openai-compatible — speaks HTTP. So the single provider with access to status codes and structured bodies is the exception, and the substrate is built for the majority case. Two consequences follow. First, a vendor rewording a message silently degrades a retryable pause into a misclassified permanent failure or vice versa, with no compile-time or test-time signal — the patterns can only be validated against strings someone once observed. Second, the same transport choice is why quota discovery needs seven bespoke source modules (claudeOAuthQuotaSource, codexQuotaSource, copilotQuotaSource, openCodeQuotaSource, antigravityQuotaSource, hostSessionQuotaSource, httpQuotaSource) scraping credential stores and undocumented endpoints. Recommendation: treat HTTP as the preferred transport wherever a vendor offers one and reserve CLI spawning for hosts that genuinely have no API, so structured status and Retry-After become the primary classification path and prose matching degrades to a last-resort fallback; and make prose classification declared, versioned data with recorded provenance per pattern (which vendor, which observed message, which date) rather than inline literals, so staleness is auditable. Note the project already reasons well about HTTP transport correctness in src/shared/providers/openAiCompatibleProvider.ts, where a documented UND_ERR_HEADERS_TIMEOUT bug drove a per-launch undici Agent with explicit deadlines — evidence the HTTP path is the better-instrumented one.

COUNTEREXAMPLE: this one is enforced only by prose. `stableStringify` does preserve array order (src/shared/stableStringify.ts:21), so the hash consequence is real; but there is no property test, no check script, and no hook. tests/audit/audit-extractors-invariants.test.ts covers edge shape, cycle detection, regex hangs, ignore files and disposition guards — no sortedness invariant; nothing under `scripts/` or `.claude/hooks/` addresses array order; coverage is only per-artifact spot assertions in unrelated tests. This repo has 2,092 non-merge commits, so the mine sees 47.8% of its own history. Measured by re-running the miner's exact argv (`git log --use-mailmap --no-merges --name-only --format=%H%x00%aN`) at max-count=1000 versus full history and re-deriving the aggregates against the extractor's own thresholds: files reaching `CHURN_HOTSPOT_FLOOR = 8` (gitHistory.ts:48) fall from 307 to 120 — the cap hides 61% of the change hotspots; files reaching `BROAD_AUTHORSHIP_FLOOR = 4` (:46) fall from 35 to 3 — 91% of the bus-factor signal is erased; files with any churn at all fall from 2,981 to 1,561. Individual counts are halved (docs/backlog.md 578 -> 348, package-lock.json 357 -> 129), which matters because both floors are ABSOLUTE counts applied to a window-relative sample: the same file crosses or misses `change_hotspot` depending purely on how much history was scanned. Those two signals are merged into the risk register (`gitHistoryRiskSignals`, gitHistory.ts:130-156) and therefore steer audit-task prioritisation. What the cap buys is measurable and small: the same single spawn either way, 387 ms full-history versus 217 ms capped on this repo — 170 ms, against an audit run measured in minutes. And the artifact already has the precedent for declaring its own bound: `skipped_cochange_commits` is carried precisely so a consumer knows the O(files^2) pair bound bit (src/shared/git.ts:141-151, 291-293), while the commit-window truncation — the bound that actually bit here — is recorded nowhere, so a downstream reader cannot tell a genuinely low-churn file from an unseen one. SECOND HALF, same root: convergence is decided by EXACT title equality. `foldChallengeRound` (src/audit/systemic/systemicChallengeLoop.ts:108-124) keys newness on `findingReEmissionKey`, which is `trim+lowercase(lens|category|title)` (src/shared/findings/dedupe.ts:300-306), and `converged` is set only by that `dry` bit — grep finds NO round cap anywhere. So a reworded restatement of a prior improvement registers as new, keeps the loop open, and costs another full serial adversary round; and the fuzzy collapse that would catch it lives in the very module the loop already imports from — `sameLensDedupe` (dedupe.ts:329: title word-Jaccard >=0.35/0.45 plus line-range or >=0.5 file-path overlap) — and ALREADY RUNS downstream in the same pipeline at src/audit/reporting/mergeFindings.ts:106, so the duplicate the loop paid a round trip for is silently collapsed at report time anyway. ### ARC-09caa494 — The one provider that writes model-returned files itself never receives the node's declared write scope, and its containment check is lexical so an in-worktree symlink escapes

TRUST BOUNDARY: `openai-compatible` is architecturally different from the agentic providers — it POSTs a packet to a `/chat/completions` endpoint and then APPLIES the returned `{files, result}` into the node's worktree itself, so the tool (not an agent's Edit tool) performs the writes.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/providers/openAiCompatibleProvider.ts`, `src/shared/io/pathContainment.ts`, `src/remediate/steps/providerNodeDispatch.ts`, `src/shared/dispatch/pathIdentity.ts`
- Details: TRUST BOUNDARY: `openai-compatible` is architecturally different from the agentic providers — it POSTs a packet to a `/chat/completions` endpoint and then APPLIES the returned `{files, result}` into the node's worktree itself, so the tool (not an agent's Edit tool) performs the writes. That makes its apply loop a first-class write boundary for untrusted model output.

WHAT IT CHECKS: root containment plus a control-plane exclusion. Each returned `file.path` goes through `safeResolveInRepo` → `resolveWithinRoot(repoRoot, candidate, { allowRoot: false })` (src/shared/providers/openAiCompatibleProvider.ts:470, :911-915), and a path under the `.audit-tools` control-plane dir is skipped. A non-contained path fails the whole launch.

TWO GAPS: (1) It never checks the node's declared `write_paths` — verified by grepping the provider: `write_paths` does not appear in the file at all, and the provider's own comment concedes the point ("The worktree branch diff is still the write-scope ground truth at merge; here we defend against a path escaping the worktree entirely", :453-455). So write scope for this provider is deferred entirely to accept-time adjudication — which DR-006 shows does not confine to declared scope on a single-block wave, and DR-007 shows is inert on the main-tree dispatch paths. Deferring to a downstream gate is sound only when that gate holds; here neither condition is guaranteed. (2) `resolveWithinRoot` is purely lexical — it calls `resolve()`/`relative()` and never `realpath` (src/shared/io/pathContainment.ts:43-58). A tracked symlink inside the worktree pointing outside it therefore resolves as contained, the write lands outside the tree, and because the symlink blob itself is unchanged the write produces no `git diff` entry — so it is invisible to the branch-diff ground truth as well as to the containment check.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: pass the node's declared `write_paths` into `LaunchFreshSessionInput` and reject a returned file outside them at apply time, so the provider that performs the write is the one that enforces the scope (fail-closed at the boundary rather than relying on a downstream gate with known holes). For the symlink half, resolve the final path with `realpath` on the existing parent directory before writing and re-run containment on the resolved result; `canonicalizeFilePath` already has a `resolveSymlinks` option, so this is a matter of threading it through rather than new machinery.

The verification is correspondingly lopsided: the audit half has ~2,362 lines of behavioural tests (tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper.test.ts 1,980, host-asset-renderer-drift.test.ts 229, a7.test.ts 153), while the remediate half appears in exactly one test — tests/shared/audit-tools-path-guard.test.ts — and only as a path literal in a scanner allowlist, so 1,760 lines of shipped install logic have no behavioural coverage at all. One host-install engine parameterized by {toolName, slashCommand, installDir, permissionAssert} plus two thin adapters collapses ~1,700 lines and makes the existing audit-side test suite bind BOTH bins.

### ARC-b94299db — Two divergent definitions of "in declared write scope" run inside the same accept: exact equality vs prefix/glob containment

INFERRED CONTRACT: "in the declared write scope" is one predicate.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/remediate/steps/dispatch/common.ts`, `src/remediate/steps/dispatch/worktreeLifecycle.ts`, `src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts`
- Details: INFERRED CONTRACT: "in the declared write scope" is one predicate. The repo treats duplicated guards as correctness work, not style — `pathContainment.ts` was created precisely because a containment check existed in five hand-rolled copies and one was subtly wrong, and project memory records "five copies of a guard hid two bugs" and "a 'lockstep' comment is the duplication tell — extract, don't drift-test".

COUNTEREXAMPLE: two different predicates decide it within a single node accept. `writeScopeViolations` uses EXACT string membership — `declared.has(rel)` after `toRepoRelative` (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/common.ts:286-290) — so a declared directory does not cover a file inside it. `isUnderWritePaths`, used by the commit's force-add pass for gitignored new files, uses PREFIX plus glob containment — `target === literalPrefix || target.startsWith(`${literalPrefix}/`)`, plus leading-wildcard handling (src/remediate/steps/dispatch/worktreeLifecycle.ts:765-787). Consequence for a block declaring `src/foo`: a worker-created `src/foo/new.ts` is IN scope for the commit force-add and OUT of scope for the write-scope gate. Today that divergence is masked by the unowned-grant of DR-006, which is what makes it a latent gap rather than a live break — remove or tighten that grant (as DR-006 recommends) and the two predicates start disagreeing visibly.

SECONDARY DIVERGENCE in the same area: `toRepoRelative` (common.ts:24-31) normalizes backslashes and strips an absolute in-root prefix, but does not strip a leading `./`, does not case-fold, and never calls `resolve`/`realpath`. Its sibling normalizer in shared, `normalizeRepoPath` (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:46-48), DOES strip `./` and case-fold. So a declared `./src/a.ts` or a mis-cased `Src/A.ts` fails to match git's `src/a.ts` on a case-insensitive filesystem — again currently absorbed by the unowned-grant.

RECOMMENDED CHANGE: extract one scope-membership predicate (declared-path list + candidate → boolean, with the glob/prefix semantics decided once) into shared and have both `writeScopeViolations` and the force-add pass call it, per the project's stated preference for extraction over drift tests. Fold the `./` strip and case-folding decision into that one normalizer so declared and actual paths are compared in a single canonical form.

### TST-6fa9de59 — Vitest's unit of parallelism is the FILE, so the suite is floored at its largest single file (268.7 s) no matter how it is sharded — and the in-file lever is untouched: 1.0% of tests are concurrent and maxConcurrency is left at the default 5

Every improvement proposed for suite latency so far operates ACROSS files (shard count, duration-balanced shard assignment, build reuse).

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: high
- Lens: tests
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `vitest.config.ts`, `tests/audit/audit-code-completion.test.ts`, `tests/audit/linux-cycle-regression.test.ts`, `tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper.test.ts` +2 more
- Details: Every improvement proposed for suite latency so far operates ACROSS files (shard count, duration-balanced shard assignment, build reuse). That lever saturates against a wall nobody priced, because `vitest --shard` partitions the file list and never splits a file: the achievable wall for ANY shard count is bounded below by max(single-file duration). Measured from the repo's own most recent full-suite ledger record (.audit-tools-profile/vitest-history.ndjson, 2026-07-29T16:49:18Z, 565 files, wallSummed 2,730,730 ms = 45.5 min, run 2,368,424 ms = 86.7%, collect 303,386 ms = 11.1%): the four heaviest files are tests/audit/audit-code-completion.test.ts 268,736 ms, tests/audit/audit-code-wrapper.test.ts 220,511 ms, tests/audit/next-step.test.ts 184,607 ms and tests/audit/linux-cycle-regression.test.ts 145,291 ms — 819,145 ms, exactly 30.0% of the whole suite, with the top ten at 44.8%. Ideal 4-way balance is 682,683 ms per shard, so at four shards the largest file is not yet binding; but the remedy of 'raise the shard count for finer granularity' hits a hard floor at 268.7 s and buys nothing past roughly ten shards. The in-file lever, which is the one that can go below that floor, is almost entirely unused, and the repo has already proved it safe. (a) Adoption is 78 `.concurrent` blocks out of 7,844 total test blocks — 1.0%. The largest file, audit-code-completion.test.ts, is FOUR tests (lines 340, 391, 467, 520) with zero `.concurrent`, i.e. ~67 s per test strictly serial — while its sibling audit-code-wrapper.test.ts runs 42 of its 43 tests as `it.concurrent`, over the same kind of CLI round-trip, so the pattern is established, reviewed and green. Both files already create per-test temp dirs via `mkdtemp`, which is the isolation that makes in-file concurrency safe; the sequential one is not sequential for a stated reason, it simply never adopted the sibling's pattern. (b) Even the files that DID adopt it are capped: vitest 3.2.6's `maxConcurrency` default is 5 (node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/defaults.B7q_naMc.js:104) and vitest.config.ts sets none of maxConcurrency / fileParallelism / maxWorkers / isolate / pool — grep for maxConcurrency across the tracked tree returns zero hits — so audit-code-wrapper.test.ts's 42 concurrent tests execute as nine sequential waves of five, on tests that are dominated by waiting on child processes rather than CPU. (c) linux-cycle-regression.test.ts is 145.3 s in a SINGLE test, so it is atomic to every scheduling mechanism the runner has: no shard count, no worker count and no concurrency setting can reduce it, only splitting the scenario. Three mechanical changes, in increasing order of effort: set `maxConcurrency` in vitest.config.ts to the real safe ceiling for IO-bound round-trip tests (the config is already the single home for suite policy, next to the deliberate isolate/setupFiles comments); convert the heavy sequential files to the `it.concurrent` form their sibling already uses; and split the one-test file. This matters beyond the 45-minute number because the same distribution sets the CI critical path and the release gate: a 30%-of-suite concentration in four files means the safety net's latency is decided by four authoring choices rather than by the runner's configuration, and the runner's configuration is where the project's own rules say a property like this belongs. Distinct from the earlier cross-file finding (build reuse plus duration-balanced sharding), whose stated target of ~121 s is unreachable for exactly the reason above, and distinct from the conceptual 'safety net costs 45-51 minutes and 7,860 tests' finding, which prices the net's total size and noise rather than the runner's parallelism unit.

### ARC-7b2ee968 — (judge-added) There is no unattended mode and no budget on operator pauses, while the stated destination is a scheduled autonomous loop

Two perspectives noted individual interactive gates as friction (DR-017, DR-018); none noticed that the gates are accumulating against a roadmap that requires their absence.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/audit/cli/args.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/hostInputPause.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts`, `CLAUDE.md`
- Details: Two perspectives noted individual interactive gates as friction (DR-017, DR-018); none noticed that the gates are accumulating against a roadmap that requires their absence. CLAUDE.md:247 states the standing plan: redesign before scheduled autonomy — architecture stabilizes first, then build a scheduled audit-remediate-PR loop on the new architecture. Nothing in the current design moves toward that. Verified: src/audit/cli/args.ts declares no unattended, non-interactive, headless or assume-yes flag of any kind, so there is no mode in which the operator-facing gates are skipped or pre-answered; src/audit/orchestrator/executors.ts declares 13 host_delegation executors (of ~25 obligations), and src/audit/orchestrator/hostInputPause.ts exists specifically to single-source WHERE the drain stops for the operator, so the pause set is a first-class concept with no ceiling attached to it. Every lap that adds a gate adds another point at which a scheduled run would halt, and there is no counter, budget, or test asserting how many operator pauses a default run contains — while the project meticulously budgets packet counts, scope files, drain steps and backlog entry lengths. Two consequences. First, the stabilize-then-automate sequencing has no exit condition: nothing distinguishes 'architecture is stable enough to automate' from 'architecture has more gates than last month'. Second, the pause count is the actual blocking constraint on the capstone, and it is invisible in planning, so work that adds a gate is never priced against the roadmap it delays. Recommendation, cheap and mostly mechanical: derive the operator-pause set from the existing data (executors.ts kind plus hostInputPause.ts) and report it as a number in the same profile history the project already keeps for verify:checks and vitest, so the trend is visible; then decide the pause budget for a default run and treat exceeding it as a design question rather than a detail. Separately, decide deliberately whether an unattended mode is the eventual shape — if it is, each new gate needs a declared non-interactive answer at the time it is added, which is far cheaper than retrofitting answers for 13 of them later.

### REL-2c3e07df — A failed credential persist after a successful refresh grant silently discards the rotated tokens and can brick the stored refresh token

refreshAndPersist runs the refresh grant (which rotates the token pair server-side) and then persists via writeCredentialsAtomic.

- Details: refreshAndPersist runs the refresh grant (which rotates the token pair server-side) and then persists via writeCredentialsAtomic. If the persist throws — on Windows, renameSync over a credentials file concurrently held open by the Claude CLI commonly fails EPERM/EBUSY — the outer catch swallows everything and returns null: the freshly granted access token is discarded instead of being used in-memory, and the on-disk refresh token has already been invalidated by the rotation, so every future refresh fails until the operator re-logs-in. The code's own double-check comment acknowledges that losing a rotation 'would invalidate the first refresh token and brick the credential', but only guards the concurrent-probe path, not the persist-failure path.

### COR-4a47b71d — consumeArrayIncoming unlinks the accepted design-review submission before it is merged/persisted — a crash in the window silently destroys host work

consumeArrayIncoming deletes the incoming file as soon as the shape check passes, before handleDesignReviewBranch merges the findings and writes design_assessment.json.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: correctness
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts:737–741`, `src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts:756–759`
- Details: consumeArrayIncoming deletes the incoming file as soon as the shape check passes, before handleDesignReviewBranch merges the findings and writes design_assessment.json. A crash or thrown write between the unlink and the design_assessment write loses the host's contract/conceptual findings with no quarantine record and no rejected_submissions note — the step re-emits with zero signal, exactly the hazard class this module elsewhere fixes. The sibling paths deliberately apply-before-delete (consumeObjectIncoming's contract, the edge-reasoning gate's 'Apply BEFORE deleting' comment, runOmittableGate), so this consume order is internally inconsistent with the module's own stated crash-retention rule.
- Evidence: 4 items (top: "src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts:738-740 - unlink(path) executes inside consumeArrayIncoming before the caller sees the value.") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### COR-7a88a3a0 — Finding identity anchor is affected_files[0], but merge passes SORT affected_files — a merged-in file that sorts before the primary silently moves the identity signature

findingIdentityFields derives the tier-1 structural anchor from finding.affected_files[0], and the module documents that identity 'stays put as additional re-emitted files are unioned into it across passes and runs'.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: correctness
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/findingIdentitySignature.ts:126–136`, `src/shared/findings/dedupe.ts:55–73`
- Details: findingIdentityFields derives the tier-1 structural anchor from finding.affected_files[0], and the module documents that identity 'stays put as additional re-emitted files are unioned into it across passes and runs'. But the merge passes that grow the union (upsertFindingByIdentity, sameLensDedupe, audit's crossLensDedupe draw) call mergeAffectedFiles with sort=true, which re-sorts affected_files by path — so when a re-emission contributes a file that sorts lexicographically before the original primary, affected_files[0] (and therefore findingIdentityKey, the stable-id hash input, and primaryPath grouping) changes. Whether a finding merged also determines whether its files were ever sorted, so the same logical finding can carry different identities across passes/runs, churning stable ids, theme references, and the coverage-ledger key the signature exists to hold still.
- Evidence: 4 items (top: "src/shared/findingIdentitySignature.ts:128 - the tier-1 anchor is whatever file happens to be at index 0 of affected_files; the docstring (lines 89-93) claims t…") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### COR-0e59a751 — Host-session near-wall band never decays: one recorded limit throttles the pool to 5% for the process lifetime

HostSessionQuotaSource.probeUsage reports the near-wall band (remaining_pct 0.05) whenever the window is open but `this.tracker != null`.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: correctness
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/shared/quota/hostSessionQuotaSource.ts:323–328`, `src/shared/quota/compositeQuotaSource.ts:74`
- Details: HostSessionQuotaSource.probeUsage reports the near-wall band (remaining_pct 0.05) whenever the window is open but `this.tracker != null`. The tracker is set on any recorded limit and is only ever cleared on escalation — there is no success path, decay, or API to reset it, and the elapsed-reset check exists only inside recordLimit. So after a single transient session limit, the source keeps answering 0.05 for its key for the rest of the process; because it is prepended in the composite cascade and the first snapshot wins, it permanently masks the proactive source's true (recovered) reading and holds the pool in the CRITICAL throttle band even long after the account has fully recovered. The source's own comment scopes the band to 'this window cycle', which the implementation does not enforce.
- Evidence: 8 items (top: "src/shared/quota/hostSessionQuotaSource.ts:323-328 - probeUsage answers near-wall (0.05) whenever tracker is non-null and the window is open; there is no check …") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### TST-5034ea59 — Ingestion requeue-fold test asserts only metrics counting while its name claims the dispatch surface — it pins the phantom-task behavior as expected

tests/audit/orchestrator-remediation.test.ts ('ingestion executor folds pending requeue tasks for uncovered files into the dispatch surface', and its dedupe sibling) verifies the fold only via audit_plan_metrics.task_count — it never asserts the folded requeue task enters bundle.audit_tasks or the derivePendingTaskPartition pending set, which is what 'dispatch surface' actually means (dispatch packets and the audit_tasks_completed gate both read only audit_tasks).

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: tests
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/audit/orchestrator/ingestionExecutors.ts:191–192`, `tests/audit/orchestrator-remediation.test.ts:1928–2064`
- Details: tests/audit/orchestrator-remediation.test.ts ('ingestion executor folds pending requeue tasks for uncovered files into the dispatch surface', and its dedupe sibling) verifies the fold only via audit_plan_metrics.task_count — it never asserts the folded requeue task enters bundle.audit_tasks or the derivePendingTaskPartition pending set, which is what 'dispatch surface' actually means (dispatch packets and the audit_tasks_completed gate both read only audit_tasks). The test therefore stays green while ingestion-born mandatory-coverage requeue tasks are metrics-only phantoms that never dispatch (see COR-001 in this packet): the important path — 'a coverage gap discovered at ingest re-dispatches' — is untested, and the current assertion pins the weaker (buggy) behavior as expected.
- Evidence: 6 items (top: "tests/audit/orchestrator-remediation.test.ts:1928-1999 - the test finds the requeue task in run.updated.requeue_tasks and checks it is 'part of the folded dispa…") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### COR-5034ea59 — Ingestion-time requeue fold is metrics-only: folded requeue tasks are never persisted into audit_tasks, so they never dispatch

runResultIngestionExecutor builds pendingRequeueTasks (mandatory coverage gaps found after ingesting results) and merges them into allDispatchTasks, but allDispatchTasks is passed ONLY to buildAuditPlanMetrics — finalBundle.audit_tasks stays the un-folded deepened set.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: correctness
- Grounding: grounded

- Details: The product's distinctive behaviour is fanning bounded work units out across many providers, models and worktrees concurrently, under quota pacing, with retries, quarantine and re-dispatch. Recommendation: at minimum emit spans in OTLP JSON with GenAI semconv attribute names so existing viewers work, and record the decision either way — the current position looks like drift rather than a choice, since no doc or backlog entry weighs it.

Measured: 1 of the 11 registered candidates has it true (gitleaks); the other 10 are denied absent a token, and this run's own external_analyzer_acquisition.json records exactly that — 13 of 14 status records skipped, one tool contributing. The one candidate admitted without consent is a `runner: binary` candidate that resolves by downloading a pinned third-party executable and running it: the live record shows the resolved command under C:\Users\...\Temp\audit-tools-bincache\gitleaks-8.21.2\gitleaks.exe. Meanwhile knip is denied — although this repo has knip ^6.23.0 in its own devDependencies, installed at node_modules/.bin/knip, and already runs it as a release gate (check:deadcode). Approving nothing and fetching-and-executing a binary is the default; using the audited repo's own pinned, already-trusted tool requires a token. (2) The bit encodes two unrelated judgments at once. knip's own comment gives its gating reason as 'needs repo config to avoid noise ... every flag here is an unverified lead, not a confirmed finding' — a LEAD-QUALITY judgment — while the same field is documented as the run-safety/consent control. Splitting the axes fixes both: derive admission from the spawn's provenance (already-resolved local/repo-pinned tool vs a fetch of remote code -> the fetch is what needs consent), and express noisiness as a separate lead-confidence policy. That also retires the curated list itself, which is a table WE hand-maintain as the primary source in backend code — the thing the project's own standing rule bans, and which admitSpawn's docblock already disclaims ('never a maintained allowlist'). Distinct from the consent-token-semantics issue (presence check / permanence / any-string-unlocks-everything): that concerns how the token is validated, this concerns which dimension the gate keys on at all, and fixing one leaves the other in place.

If a concurrent stealer completes its own steal and wx-recreates a FRESH lock between another acquirer's stat and readFile, the second acquirer captures the fresh holder's token as its 'stale token', wins the (already-released) claim, passes the content check trivially, and unlinks a live, fresh lock — a double-hold. The heartbeat cannot help: the unlink check compares content only, never mtime. The window is narrow (the stat->read gap must straddle the first stealer's unlink->recreate) but this lock guards quota-state and credential read-modify-writes, so the failure mode is concurrent writers and a lost update on those files. A cheap close: after winning the steal claim, re-stat and abort unless the mtime is still older than STALE_LOCK_MS in addition to the token match.

spec/audit/dependency-map.md row for design_assessment.json lists BOTH design_review_contract and design_review_conceptual as consumers of the same single upstream, and there is no edge between the two passes.

- Confidence: medium
- Lens: performance
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts`, `spec/audit/dependency-map.md`, `src/audit/cli/nextStepHelpers.ts`
- Details: spec/audit/dependency-map.md row for design_assessment.json lists BOTH design_review_contract and design_review_conceptual as consumers of the same single upstream, and there is no edge between the two passes. nextStepHelpers.ts handles them as two independent 'only this pass still needed' branches, and no conceptual prompt reads contract output - verified: design-review-conceptual-p1-prompt.md contains no reference to contract findings, and the two design-review-snapshots carry each pass's OWN prior_findings, never the sibling's. Yet PRIORITY hard-orders design_review_contract_completed before design_review_conceptual_completed, so the whole contract pass must complete and be ingested before the conceptual 5-way fan-out is even dispatched. Since both are host_delegation dispatch pauses over the same frozen bundle, the review phase costs two serial host round trips where one step could dispatch all six agents (1 contract + 5 perspectives) concurrently and ingest them together - roughly halving the review phase's wall time, which is the dominant phase of a deep run. The general improvement is bigger than this one pair: PRIORITY is a flat total order over an obligation set whose real constraints are a partial order, so every set of DAG-siblings is needlessly serialized. Letting the scan select a concurrently-dispatchable FRONTIER (all unsatisfied obligations with no unsatisfied ancestor) rather than a single highest-priority element preserves the 'upstream-valid before downstream-refresh' invariant exactly while recovering the parallelism the DAG already permits.

### ARC-7b2ee968-2 — The emitted resume command inlines a ~400-char escaped-JSON blob the host must reproduce byte-exactly

Every step prompt ends with the command the host must run next, and that command carries the auditor descriptor as an inline escaped-JSON literal — around 400 characters of backslash-escaped JSON, present in 6 of the recorded step prompts under .audit-tools/audit/steps/.

- Severity: medium
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `src/audit/cli/args.ts`, `src/audit/cli/nextStepCommand.ts`, `src/audit/cli/envelope.ts`
- Details: Every step prompt ends with the command the host must run next, and that command carries the auditor descriptor as an inline escaped-JSON literal — around 400 characters of backslash-escaped JSON, present in 6 of the recorded step prompts under .audit-tools/audit/steps/. The tool already holds this value and re-serializes it into the prompt, so the escaping is the tool's choice, not something forced by the host. This lands on the shell where it is most fragile. The repo's own conventions carry a rule for exactly this hazard (PowerShell JSON generation must be statement-safe: assign first, then pipe) and a hook guarding inline-JSON traps, on a Windows-primary machine. A grep for an alternative transport (--auditor-file, descriptor-file, auditorPath) finds none — the escaped literal is the only way in, and src/audit/cli/args.ts:246 reads it straight from the flag. This is also the auditor-agnostic invariant applied to the tool's own output: that invariant says a workflow must never depend on the host getting something right by care, and asking a host to relay 400 characters of nested escaping through an arbitrary shell is precisely such a place. It is unreadable at a glance, so a corruption in the middle of the blob is invisible until it fails to parse. Recommendation: write the descriptor to the step directory where current-step.json already lives and emit --auditor-file <path> in the prompt, keeping --auditor for programmatic callers. The emitted command becomes short enough to read and verify at a glance, and nothing has to survive a shell's quoting rules.

- Confidence: high

- Files: `src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/executorRunners.ts`, `src/shared/engine/obligationEngine.ts`, `scripts/check-doc-code-citations.mjs`
- Details: Two small items worth fixing together because both are the failure mode the gate apparatus exists to prevent, appearing inside the apparatus itself. First, FRICTION_CAPTURE_OBLIGATION_ID is a member of PRIORITY (src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:59) but is never derived by deriveAuditState, so the scan can never select it — its obligation was replaced by the terminal triage gate described in DR-017. src/audit/orchestrator/executorRunners.ts:215-218 documents this outright, saying the executor is retained for schema compatibility but is unreachable. The reason it must be retained is assertExecutorRegistryCoversPriority (nextStep.ts:71-88), a good load-time invariant requiring every PRIORITY id to own exactly one executor — which here forces dead code to stay alive to satisfy a guard about live code. The honest resolution is to remove the id from PRIORITY and delete the executor with it in one commit, per the repo's own atomic-replace rule; the guard then passes on a smaller, true registry. (DR-011's unified obligation record subsumes this: a record set cannot carry an id with no derive.) Second, the doc comment in src/shared/engine/obligationEngine.ts:18 directs the reader to spec/a3-a4-engine-unification-plan.md for the engine's design, and that file does not exist anywhere in the tree. This survives despite check:doc-code-citations, because that gate scans tracked markdown for citations into code and has no inverse — code comments citing docs are unchecked. Given how much of this codebase's reasoning lives in long comments pointing at specs, extending the existing gate to also resolve repo-path citations found in src/** comments is a small addition to a script that already owns the tracked-file resolution logic, and it closes the direction that currently rots silently.

### PRF-c4b7bd17 — src is fully typechecked three times per verify-and-commit cycle with incremental and composite both off, so no typecheck work is ever reused

tsconfig.base.json sets no incremental and no composite, and there are no project references anywhere; tsconfig.test.json re-declares include: ['src','tests'], so it re-parses and re-checks the entire 129k-line src tree from scratch rather than consuming src's emitted declarations.

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Lens: performance
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `tsconfig.base.json`, `tsconfig.test.json`, `tsconfig.json`, `package.json`
- Details: tsconfig.base.json sets no incremental and no composite, and there are no project references anywhere; tsconfig.test.json re-declares include: ['src','tests'], so it re-parses and re-checks the entire 129k-line src tree from scratch rather than consuming src's emitted declarations. The result is three full passes over src per cycle: check:tests (measured 5,372 ms) and build (measured 5,028 ms) both inside verify:checks, plus the pre-commit gate's own npm run check (tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit) on every commit - and each pass starts cold because nothing is cached (no .tsbuildinfo exists on disk). Turning tsconfig.json into a composite project, referencing it from tsconfig.test.json, and enabling incremental makes the test typecheck consume dist .d.ts instead of re-checking src, and makes repeat runs near-instant on an unchanged tree. This is the standard tsc project-references arrangement, needs no new dependency, and is worth roughly 10 s per verify plus the full cost of the pre-commit check on every commit - the highest-frequency gate in the repo.

### ARC-f6b056c5 — Terminology defects at the centre of the loop: bounded step is defined by retraction in four homes, and obligation names two unrelated lattices with inverted ordering conventions

Two perspectives found two instances of one cheap, high-comprehension-leverage class, so they merge.

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Files: `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/project-philosophy.md`, `spec/audit/entrypoint-contract.md`, `src/remediate/steps/contractPipeline.ts` +2 more
- Details: Two perspectives found two instances of one cheap, high-comprehension-leverage class, so they merge. First, the invariant reads: one bounded step per invocation equals a fold-aware drain, not a single obligation — the term's definition is a retraction of the term. The same correction is restated in docs/project-philosophy.md (A1), again in CLAUDE.md's audit-architecture section, and again in spec/audit/entrypoint-contract.md; fold-aware appears across 9 files including four test names. Any name that needs three sentences of 'this does not mean what it says' has selected the wrong name, and each new home inherits the correction, which is why there are four copies. The underlying behavior takes one clause to state accurately: a call keeps draining deterministic work and stops at the first point it needs you. Bounded step fails because it implies exactly one; fold-aware drain fails because fold is undefined jargon and aware carries no information. Second, the word obligation carries two unrelated meanings: in the engine it is a unit of orchestrator progress (src/shared/engine/obligationEngine.ts, selected by an ordered priority array), while in the contract pipeline it is a derived requirement on a change (src/remediate/steps/contractPipeline.ts:2833 declares a LOCAL type ObligationKind of invariant/behavioral/structural/test, unrelated to the engine type). Both carry an ordering array and the two conventions are inverted: PRIORITY in src/audit/orchestrator/nextStep.ts:25 is highest-priority-first (the scan returns the first actionable entry), while OBLIGATION_KIND_PRIORITY in contractPipeline.ts:2836 is documented as higher index equals higher priority and is consumed via indexOf comparison. A reader who has internalized one convention will misread the other, and the shared word invites exactly that transfer. Recommendation: rename the drain concept to what it does (pause-bounded invocation, or plainly drains-until-it-needs-you) so the retraction has nothing to retract and is deleted from all four homes at once; rename the contract-pipeline concept (RequirementKind / REQUIREMENT_KIND_RANK) and express rank as an explicit numeric field rather than array position in either place, so one ordering convention holds repo-wide.
- Evidence: 4 items (top: "runtime:flow:flow:host:audit-orchestration-loop: confirmed — Deterministic runtime command succeeded: npm test") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### REL-84f1a967 — withClaimHeartbeat settles only the LAST tick's heartbeat; an earlier in-flight heartbeat can outlive the guarded call

The teardown guarantee ('Settle any in-flight heartbeat write so none outlives the guarded call') is implemented by awaiting a single `pendingHeartbeat` variable that each interval tick OVERWRITES.

- Severity: low
- Confidence: high
- Lens: reliability
- Grounding: grounded
- Impact: A straggler heartbeat's withFileLock IO (lock-file creation, registry read) can fire against a directory the caller is tearing down; on Windows this is an EBUSY/EPERM flake source. Fix direction: chain (pendingHeartbeat = pendingHeartbeat.then(...)) or collect unsettled promises.
- Files: `src/shared/quota/claimLease.ts:77–104`
- Details: The teardown guarantee ('Settle any in-flight heartbeat write so none outlives the guarded call') is implemented by awaiting a single `pendingHeartbeat` variable that each interval tick OVERWRITES. If tick N's heartbeat is still pending (e.g. slow withFileLock acquisition under contention, whose backoff reaches 500ms and stale-lock window 30s) when tick N+1 fires, the reference to N's promise is lost and the finally block awaits only N+1. Tick N's registry read-modify-write can then land after the caller has released the claim or begun run-dir teardown — the exact race the tracking comment says this variable exists to prevent. Impact is bounded (heartbeat is token-checked, so a post-release write no-ops), but the residual lock-file create/IO can still race directory teardown and the stated invariant does not hold.
- Evidence: 4 items (top: "src/shared/quota/claimLease.ts:81-94 - each tick reassigns pendingHeartbeat, discarding any still-pending prior promise instead of chaining or collecting it.") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### COR-2c7140b6 — ClaimRegistry.claim hands the live owner's token to the losing contender, defeating the token-check capability model

On contention, claim() returns `{ acquired: false, heldBy: existing.ownerToken }` — the opaque token that release(), heartbeat(), and stale-reclaim survival are all gated on.

- Severity: low
- Confidence: medium
- Lens: correctness
- Grounding: grounded
- Impact: The single-grant invariant degrades from mechanically enforced to cooperatively honored: any loop that lost a claim race holds everything needed to drop or refresh the winner's claim.
- Files: `src/shared/quota/claimRegistry.ts:128–130`, `src/shared/quota/claimRegistry.ts:248–253`
- Details: On contention, claim() returns `{ acquired: false, heldBy: existing.ownerToken }` — the opaque token that release(), heartbeat(), and stale-reclaim survival are all gated on. Every contender therefore receives the exact capability the token checks exist to withhold: a peer loop (or any code that stores the ClaimResult) can release or heartbeat a claim it never owned, which is precisely the 'stale-observation racer clobbers a live owner' scenario the token-checked release documents itself as preventing. If the caller needs to display or route on the holder's identity, poolId is the non-capability identity already stored on the record.
- Evidence: 4 items (top: "src/shared/quota/claimRegistry.ts:129 - the losing contender receives existing.ownerToken verbatim.") — see audit-findings.json for the full list

### ARC-60a52950-4 — What is genuinely right — the mechanically-enforced primitives and the degenerate-case pattern are the template every finding above should be closed against

All five perspectives independently ended on this note, which is itself evidence: the fundamental approach is sound and the gaps are places it has not yet been applied.

- Severity: info
- Confidence: high
- Lens: architecture
- Grounding: grounded
- Systemic: yes
- Files: `src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts`, `src/remediate/review/autonomousGate.ts`, `src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts`, `src/audit/orchestrator/advance.ts` +6 more
- Details: All five perspectives independently ended on this note, which is itself evidence: the fundamental approach is sound and the gaps are places it has not yet been applied. This finding merges their credit lists because it changes what the other 44 are asking for — apply your own proven pattern consistently, not rebuild. (1) Enforcement rather than instruction, where it exists, is genuinely hard to fool: quote grounding re-reads a verbatim span from disk and content-matches it, whitespace/CRLF-normalized and matched on content NOT line numbers, so later edits do not false-fail a still-valid quote (src/shared/validation/findingGrounding.ts:158-193) — DR-007 argues only that the property it establishes is weaker than the product claims, not that the mechanism is wrong. The autonomous approval gate is fail-closed by construction: a CLOSED positive enumeration of four provably-safe change kinds, anything unclassifiable excluded, no severity/cost escape hatch, no durable rejection (src/remediate/review/autonomousGate.ts:26-70). The read-only command allowlist is real default-deny with per-executable flag policies, an enumerated read-only git subcommand set, no shell, a 60s timeout with SIGKILL escalation and 256 KiB output cap (src/shared/tooling/allowlistedExec.ts) — DR-001(c) is a one-line hole in an otherwise correct design. Termination is engineered, not hoped for: MAX_DRAIN_STEPS is a graceful stop explicitly coupled to the engine's throwing backstop at +2 so the graceful cap always trips first however the constant is retuned (src/audit/orchestrator/advance.ts:42-48). Cost is bounded by construction: frontier expansion halts at a file budget, skips high-fan-in hubs, drops low-confidence edges, and is deterministic (src/audit/orchestrator/scope.ts:40-52). And knipGraphCrosscheck refuses to promote a dead-code lead to a verdict when the relevant analyzer did not run (:137-139) — exactly the fidelity instinct DR-016 asks the report to inherit. (2) The degenerate-case pattern is the shape to generalize: src/shared/dispatch/unifiedRolling.ts embeds audit as the READ-ONLY degenerate case — one level of read-only nodes that the sub-wave machinery collapses to a no-op — and that degenerate case costs nothing: no second code path, no parity test, no memo. src/shared/fileIntegrity.ts is a genuine higher-order core parameterized by record accessors, so the audit and remediate sides are different INPUTS to one algorithm rather than two implementations. src/audit/orchestrator/dependencyMap.ts derives the forward view by inverting the single hand-authored adjacency so the two can never drift, and constrains its keys to a type derived from ARTIFACT_DEFINITIONS so a stale filename is a compile error. (3) The acquire-and-normalize instinct, where applied, is better than what a reviewer would have recommended: JSON Schema is GENERATED from zod rather than hand-maintained, with a drift test on the committed artifacts; the TOML and YAML parsers use vetted libraries and each carries a docstring recording the bug class its hand-rolled predecessor had; the JS/TS graph layer uses the real TypeScript Compiler API resolved from the AUDITED repo's own typescript first and degrades to a regex floor with confidence encoding the difference; gitignore semantics are deliberately NOT reimplemented (one batched git check-ignore); undici is chosen with the rationale written down at the point of use, that HTTP transport is correctness-sensitive enough to acquire rather than own; and language metadata is synced from linguist-languages rather than hand-maintained. (4) The product's own output respects a reader's attention better than the repo's internal documentation does: rendered host prompts are 19-370 lines with one clear task, absolute paths, an explicit stop condition and the exact next command. The generalizable lesson across all four groups: every place this project achieved elegance did so by finding the PARAMETER that made two things one (a level count, a record accessor, an adjacency direction, a confidence weight), and every place it did not, it added a table and a test to keep two things agreeing. The former is available in each of DR-011, DR-012, DR-015, DR-023 and DR-024. Two residual nits worth folding into any touch of these files: the remediate fileIntegrity side hand-doubles the sync/async axis four times, and the two sides return the same record shape under different field names.
